preface.title: Introduction
preface.para: The calendar extension presents a series of functions to simplify converting between different calendar formats. The intermediary or standard it is based on is the Julian Day Count. The Julian Day Count is a count of days starting from January 1st, 4713 B.C. To convert between calendar systems, you must first convert to Julian Day Count, then to the calendar system of your choice. Julian Day Count is very different from the Julian Calendar! For more information on Julian Day Count, visit http://www.hermetic.ch/cal_stud/jdn.htm. For more information on calendar systems visit http://www.fourmilab.ch/documents/calendar/. Excerpts from this page are included in these instructions, and are in quotes.

section.title: Installation
section.para: To get these functions to work, you have to compile PHP with --enable-calendar.
section.simpara: The Windows version of PHP has built-in support for this extension. You do not need to load any additional extensions in order to use these functions.

appendix.title: Predefined Constants
appendix.simpara: The constants below are defined by this extension, and will only be available when the extension has either been compiled into PHP or dynamically loaded at runtime.

listitem.simpara: For easter_days: calculate Easter for years before 1753 according to the Julian calendar, and for later years according to the Gregorian calendar.
For easter_days: calculate Easter for years before 1583 according to the Julian calendar, and for later years according to the Gregorian calendar.
For easter_days: calculate Easter according to the proleptic Gregorian calendar.
For easter_days: calculate Easter according to the Julian calendar.
For cal_days_in_month, cal_from_jd, cal_info and cal_to_jd: use the proleptic Gregorian calendar.
For cal_days_in_month, cal_from_jd, cal_info and cal_to_jd: use the Julian calendar.
For cal_days_in_month, cal_from_jd, cal_info and cal_to_jd: use the Jewish calendar.
For cal_days_in_month, cal_from_jd, cal_info and cal_to_jd: use the French Republican calendar.
The number of available calendars.
For jdtojewish: adds a geresh symbol (which resembles a single-quote mark) as thousands separator to the year number.
For jdtojewish: adds the word alafim as thousands separator to the year number.
For jdtojewish: add a gershayim symbol (which resembles a double-quote mark) before the final letter of the day and year numbers.
For jddayofweek: the day of the week as int, where 0 means Sunday and 6 means Saturday.
For jddayofweek: the abbreviated English name of the day of the week.
For jddayofweek: the English name of the day of the week.
For jdmonthname: the abbreviated Gregorian month name.
For jdmonthname: the Gregorian month name.
For jdmonthname: the abbreviated Julian month name.
For jdmonthname: the Julian month name.
For jdmonthname: the Jewish month name.
For jdmonthname: the French Republican month name.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Return the number of days in a month for a given year and calendar

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: This function will return the number of days in the month of year for the specified calendar.

listitem.para: Calendar to use for calculation
Month in the selected calendar
Year in the selected calendar

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The length in days of the selected month in the given calendar

example.title: cal_days_in_month example
example.programlisting: <?php $number = cal_days_in_month(CAL_GREGORIAN, 8, 2003); // 31 echo "There were {$number} days in August 2003"; ?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts from Julian Day Count to a supported calendar

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: cal_from_jd converts the Julian day given in julian_day into a date of the specified calendar. Supported calendar values are CAL_GREGORIAN, CAL_JULIAN, CAL_JEWISH and CAL_FRENCH.

listitem.para: Julian day as integer
Calendar to convert to

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns an array containing calendar information like month, day, year, day of week (dow), abbreviated and full names of weekday and month and the date in string form "month/day/year". The day of week ranges from 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday).

example.title: cal_from_jd example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$today = unixtojd(mktime(0, 0, 0, 8, 16, 2003));
print_r(cal_from_jd($today, CAL_GREGORIAN));
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns information about a particular calendar

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: cal_info returns information on the specified calendar.

Calendar information is returned as an array containing the elements calname, calsymbol, month, abbrevmonth and maxdaysinmonth. The names of the different calendars which can be used as calendar are as follows:
0 or CAL_GREGORIAN - Gregorian Calendar
1 or CAL_JULIAN - Julian Calendar
2 or CAL_JEWISH - Jewish Calendar
3 or CAL_FRENCH - French Revolutionary Calendar
If no calendar is specified information on all supported calendars is returned as an array.

listitem.para: Calendar to return information for. If no calendar is specified information about all calendars is returned.

example.title: cal_info example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$info = cal_info(0);
print_r($info);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts from a supported calendar to Julian Day Count

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: cal_to_jd calculates the Julian day count for a date in the specified calendar. Supported calendars are CAL_GREGORIAN, CAL_JULIAN, CAL_JEWISH and CAL_FRENCH.

listitem.para: Calendar to convert from, one of CAL_GREGORIAN, CAL_JULIAN, CAL_JEWISH or CAL_FRENCH.
The month as a number, the valid range depends on the calendar
The day as a number, the valid range depends on the calendar
The year as a number, the valid range depends on the calendar

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: A Julian Day number.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Get Unix timestamp for local midnight on Easter of a given year

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the Unix timestamp corresponding to midnight on Easter of the given year.

The date of Easter Day was defined by the Council of Nicaea in AD325 as the Sunday after the first full moon which falls on or after the Spring Equinox. The Equinox is assumed to always fall on 21st March, so the calculation reduces to determining the date of the full moon and the date of the following Sunday. The algorithm used here was introduced around the year 532 by Dionysius Exiguus. Under the Julian Calendar (for years before 1753) a simple 19-year cycle is used to track the phases of the Moon. Under the Gregorian Calendar (for years after 1753 - devised by Clavius and Lilius, and introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in October 1582, and into Britain and its then colonies in September 1752) two correction factors are added to make the cycle more accurate.

listitem.para: The year must be a number between 1970 and 2037 for 32-bit systems, or between 1970 and 2,000,000,000 for 64-bit systems. If omitted or null, defaults to the current year according to the local time.
Allows Easter dates to be calculated based on the Julian calendar when set to CAL_EASTER_ALWAYS_JULIAN. See also calendar constants.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The easter date as a unix timestamp.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: A ValueError is thrown if the year is earlier than 1970 or later than 2037 when running on a 32-bit system, or later than 2,000,000,000 on a 64-bit system.

row.entry: On 64-bit systems, the year parameter now accepts values within the range of 1970 to 2,000,000,000.
A ValueError is now thrown when year is outside the allowed range. Previously, an E_WARNING was raised and the function returned false.

example.title: easter_date example
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo date("M-d-Y", easter_date(1999)); // Apr-04-1999 echo date("M-d-Y", easter_date(2000)); // Apr-23-2000 echo date("M-d-Y", easter_date(2001)); // Apr-15-2001
?>

example.title: Using easter_date with DateTime
example.programlisting:
<?php

$timestamp = easter_date(2023);

$datetime = new \DateTime();
$datetime->setTimestamp($timestamp);

echo $datetime->format('M-d-Y'); // Apr-09-2023

?>

note.para: easter_date relies on your system's C library time functions, rather than using PHP's internal date and time functions. As a consequence, easter_date uses the TZ environment variable to determine the time zone it should operate in, rather than using PHP's default time zone, which may result in unexpected behaviour when using this function in conjunction with other date functions in PHP.
As a workaround, you can use the easter_days with DateTime and DateInterval to calculate the start of Easter in your PHP time zone as follows:

informalexample.programlisting:
<?php
function get_easter_datetime($year) {
    $base = new DateTime("$year-03-21");
    $days = easter_days($year);

    return $base->add(new DateInterval("P{$days}D"));
}

foreach (range(2012, 2015) as $year) {
    printf("Easter in %d is on %s\n",
           $year,
           get_easter_datetime($year)->format('F j'));
}
?>
informalexample.screen: Easter in 2012 is on April 8 Easter in 2013 is on March 31 Easter in 2014 is on April 20 Easter in 2015 is on April 5

simplelist.member: easter_days for calculating Easter before 1970 or after 2037

refnamediv.refpurpose: Get number of days after March 21 on which Easter falls for a given year

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the number of days after March 21 on which Easter falls for a given year. If no year is specified, the current year is assumed.
This function can be used instead of easter_date to calculate Easter for years which fall outside the range of Unix timestamps (i.e. before 1970 or after 2037).

The date of Easter Day was defined by the Council of Nicaea in AD325 as the Sunday after the first full moon which falls on or after the Spring Equinox. The Equinox is assumed to always fall on 21st March, so the calculation reduces to determining the date of the full moon and the date of the following Sunday. The algorithm used here was introduced around the year 532 by Dionysius Exiguus. Under the Julian Calendar (for years before 1753) a simple 19-year cycle is used to track the phases of the Moon. Under the Gregorian Calendar (for years after 1753 - devised by Clavius and Lilius, and introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in October 1582, and into Britain and its then colonies in September 1752) two correction factors are added to make the cycle more accurate.

listitem.para: The year as a positive number. If omitted or null, defaults to the current year according to the local time.
Allows Easter dates to be calculated based on the Gregorian calendar during the years 1582 - 1752 when set to CAL_EASTER_ROMAN. See the calendar constants for more valid constants.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The number of days after March 21st that the Easter Sunday is in the given year.

example.title: easter_days example
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo easter_days(1999); // 14, i.e. April 4 echo easter_days(1492); // 32, i.e. April 22 echo easter_days(1913); // 2, i.e. March 23
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts a date from the French Republican Calendar to a Julian Day Count

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Converts a date from the French Republican Calendar to a Julian Day Count.
These routines only convert dates in years 1 through 14 (Gregorian dates 22 September 1792 through 22 September 1806). This more than covers the period when the calendar was in use.

listitem.para: The month as a number from 1 (for Vendémiaire) to 13 (for the period of 5-6 days at the end of each year)
The day as a number from 1 to 30
The year as a number between 1 and 14

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The julian day for the given french revolution date as an integer.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts a Gregorian date to Julian Day Count

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: The valid range for the Gregorian calendar is from November 25, 4714 B.C. to at least December 31, 9999 A.D.

Although this function can handle dates all the way back to 4714 B.C., such use may not be meaningful. The Gregorian calendar was not instituted until October 15, 1582 (or October 5, 1582 in the Julian calendar). Some countries did not accept it until much later. For example, Britain converted in 1752, The USSR in 1918 and Greece in 1923. Most European countries used the Julian calendar prior to the Gregorian.

listitem.para: The month as a number from 1 (for January) to 12 (for December)
The day as a number from 1 to 31. If the month has less days then given, overflow occurs; see the example below.

The year as a number between -4714 and 9999. Negative numbers mean years B.C., positive numbers mean years A.D. Note that there is no year 0; December 31, 1 B.C. is immediately followed by January 1, 1 A.D.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The julian day for the given gregorian date as an integer. Dates outside the valid range return 0.

example.title: Calendar functions
example.programlisting:
<?php
$jd = gregoriantojd(10, 11, 1970);
echo "$jd\n";
$gregorian = jdtogregorian($jd);
echo "$gregorian\n";
?>

example.title: Overflow behavior
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo gregoriantojd(2, 31, 2018), PHP_EOL,
     gregoriantojd(3,  3, 2018), PHP_EOL;
?>

refsect1.para: Converts a Julian Day Count to the Jewish Calendar.

If the hebrew parameter is set to true, the flags parameter is used for Hebrew, ISO-8859-8 encoded string based, output format.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts a Julian Day Count to a Julian Calendar Date

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Converts Julian Day Count to a string containing the Julian Calendar Date in the format of "month/day/year".

refsect1.para: The julian date as a string in the form "month/day/year"

refnamediv.refpurpose: Convert Julian Day to Unix timestamp

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: This function will return a Unix timestamp corresponding to the Julian Day given in julian_day. The time returned is UTC.

listitem.para: A julian day number between 2440588 and 106751993607888 on 64bit systems, or between 2440588 and 2465443 on 32bit systems.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The unix timestamp for the start (midnight, not noon) of the given Julian day

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: If julian_day is outside of the allowed range, a ValueError is thrown.

The upper limit of julian_day has been extended. Previously, it was 2465342 regardless of the architecture.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts a date in the Jewish Calendar to Julian Day Count

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Although this function can handle dates all the way back to the year 1 (3761 B.C.), such use may not be meaningful. The Jewish calendar has been in use for several thousand years, but in the early days there was no formula to determine the start of a month. A new month was started when the new moon was first observed.

listitem.para: The month as a number from 1 to 13, where 1 means Tishri, 13 means Elul, and 6 and 7 mean Adar in regular years, but Adar I and Adar II, respectively, in leap years.
The day as a number from 1 to 30. If the month has only 29 days, the first day of the following month is assumed.
The year as a number between 1 and 9999

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The julian day for the given jewish date as an integer.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts a Julian Calendar date to Julian Day Count

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Valid Range for Julian Calendar 4713 B.C. to 9999 A.D.

Although this function can handle dates all the way back to 4713 B.C., such use may not be meaningful. The calendar was created in 46 B.C., but the details did not stabilize until at least 8 A.D., and perhaps as late as the 4th century. Also, the beginning of a year varied from one culture to another - not all accepted January as the first month.

caution.para: Remember, the current calendar system being used worldwide is the Gregorian calendar. gregoriantojd can be used to convert such dates to their Julian Day count.

listitem.para: The month as a number from 1 (for January) to 12 (for December)
The day as a number from 1 to 31
The year as a number between -4713 and 9999

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The julian day for the given julian date as an integer.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Convert Unix timestamp to Julian Day

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Return the Julian Day for a Unix timestamp (seconds since 1.1.1970), or for the current day if no timestamp is given. Either way, the time is regarded as local time (not UTC).

listitem.para: A unix timestamp to convert.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: A julian day number as integer, or false on failure.

preface.title: Introduction
preface.para: The DateTimeImmutable and related classes allow you represent date/time information. The objects can be created by passing in a string presentation of date/time information, or from the current system's time.
A rich set of methods is supplied to modify and format this information as well, including handling timezones and DST transitions.

The date/time features in PHP implements the ISO 8601 calendar, which is a proleptic Gregorian calendar which implements the current leap-day rules from before the Gregorian calendar was in place, and also includes the year 0 as the year number in between -1 BCE and 1 CE. Leap seconds are not supported.

The date and time information is internally stored as a 64-bit number so all conceivably useful dates (including negative years) are supported. The range is from about 292 billion years in the past to the same in the future.

note.simpara: The timezones referenced in this section can be found in the .

section.title: Installation
section.simpara: There is no installation needed to use these functions; they are part of the PHP core.

note.title: Getting the latest timezone database
note.para: The latest version of the timezone database can be installed via PECL's timezonedb.

section.title: Runtime Configuration
section.simpara: The behaviour of these functions is affected by settings in php.ini.
section.para:
Date/Time Configuration Options
Name Default Changeable Changelog
date.default_latitude "31.7667" INI_ALL
date.default_longitude "35.2333" INI_ALL
date.sunrise_zenith "90.833333" INI_ALL Prior to PHP 8.0.0, the default was "90.583333"
date.sunset_zenith "90.833333" INI_ALL Prior to PHP 8.0.0, the default was "90.583333"
date.timezone "UTC" INI_ALL From PHP 8.2, a warning is emitted when setting this to an invalid value or an empty string.
For further details and definitions of the INI_* modes, see the .
section.simpara: Here's a short explanation of the configuration directives.

listitem.para: The default latitude ranging from 0 at the equator, to +90 northward, and -90 southward.
The default longitude ranging from 0 at the prime meridian to +180 eastward and −180 westward.
The default sunrise zenith.
The default value is 90°50'. The additional 50' is due to two components: the Sun's radius, which is 16', and the atmospheric refraction, which is 34'.
The default sunset zenith.

The default timezone used by all date/time functions. The precedence order for which timezone is used if none is explicitly mentioned is described in the date_default_timezone_get page. See for a list of supported timezones.

note.simpara: The first four configuration options are currently only used by date_sunrise and date_sunset.

appendix.title: Predefined Constants
appendix.para: The DATE_* constants are defined and offer standard date representations, which can be used along with the date format functions (like date).

variablelist.title: Available returnFormat for date_sunrise and date_sunset

warning.simpara: These constants are deprecated as of PHP 8.4.0. The corresponding date_sunrise and date_sunset functions are deprecated as of PHP 8.1.0.

listitem.simpara: Timestamp
Hours:minutes (example: 08:02)
Hours as floating point number (example 8.75)
Atom (example: 2005-08-15T15:52:01+00:00); compatible with ISO-8601, RFC 3339, and XML Schema
HTTP Cookies (example: Monday, 15-Aug-2005 15:52:01 UTC)

note.simpara: This format is not compatible with ISO-8601, but is left this way for backward compatibility reasons. Use DATE_ISO8601_EXPANDED, DATE_ATOM for compatibility with ISO-8601 instead (ref ISO8601:2004 section 4.3.3 clause d).
This format allows for year ranges outside of ISO-8601's normal range of 0000-9999 by always including a sign character. It also ensures that the timezone part (+01:00) is compatible with ISO-8601.

listitem.simpara: RFC 822 (example: Mon, 15 Aug 05 15:52:01 +0000)
RFC 850 (example: Monday, 15-Aug-05 15:52:01 UTC)
RFC 7231 (as of PHP 7.0.19 and 7.1.5) (example: Sat, 30 Apr 2016 17:52:13 GMT)
Same as DATE_ATOM.
RFC 3339 EXTENDED format (example: 2005-08-15T15:52:01.000+00:00)
RSS (example: Mon, 15 Aug 2005 15:52:01 +0000). Alias of DATE_RFC1123.
World Wide Web Consortium (example: 2005-08-15T15:52:01+00:00). Alias of DATE_RFC3339.

section.title: Date/Time Arithmetic
section.para: The following examples show some pitfalls of Date/Time arithmetic with regard to DST transitions and months having different numbers of days.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::add/sub add intervals which cover elapsed time
example.simpara: Adding PT24H over a DST transition will appear to add 23/25 hours (for most timezones).
example.programlisting:
<?php
$dt = new DateTimeImmutable("2015-11-01 00:00:00", new DateTimeZone("America/New_York"));
echo "Start: ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
$dt = $dt->add(new DateInterval("PT3H"));
echo "End:   ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::modify and strtotime increment or decrement individual component values
example.simpara: Adding +24 hours over a DST transition will add exactly 24 hours as seen in the date/time string (unless the start or end time is on a transition point).
example.programlisting:
<?php
$dt = new DateTimeImmutable("2015-11-01 00:00:00", new DateTimeZone("America/New_York"));
echo "Start: ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
$dt = $dt->modify("+24 hours");
echo "End:   ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;

example.title: DateInterval::createFromDateString creates intervals which increment or decrement component values
example.simpara: DateInterval::createFromDateString uses the date/time parser, and the time part of the resulting interval increments or decrements the individual component values. For an interval created with DateInterval::__construct the time part covers elapsed time instead, so the two are not interchangeable when a timezone transition falls within that time part. The date part is applied the same way by both, so P1D and 1 day always give the same result.
example.programlisting:
<?php
$dt = new DateTimeImmutable("2015-11-01 00:00:00", new DateTimeZone("America/New_York"));
echo "Start:    ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
echo "PT24H:    ", $dt->add(new DateInterval("PT24H"))->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
echo "24 hours: ", $dt->add(DateInterval::createFromDateString("24 hours"))->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;

example.title: Adding or subtracting times can over- or underflow dates
example.simpara: Like where January 31st + 1 month will result in March 2nd (leap year) or 3rd (normal year).
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo "Normal year:\n"; // February has 28 days
$dt = new DateTimeImmutable("2015-01-31 00:00:00", new DateTimeZone("America/New_York"));
echo "Start: ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
$dt = $dt->modify("+1 month");
echo "End:   ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;

echo "Leap year:\n"; // February has 29 days
$dt = new DateTimeImmutable("2016-01-31 00:00:00", new DateTimeZone("America/New_York"));
echo "Start: ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
$dt = $dt->modify("+1 month");
echo "End:   ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
example.simpara: To get the last day of the next month (i.e. to prevent the overflow), the last day of format is available.
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo "Normal year:\n"; // February has 28 days
$dt = new DateTimeImmutable("2015-01-31 00:00:00", new DateTimeZone("America/New_York"));
echo "Start: ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
$dt = $dt->modify("last day of next month");
echo "End:   ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;

echo "Leap year:\n"; // February has 29 days
$dt = new DateTimeImmutable("2016-01-31 00:00:00", new DateTimeZone("America/New_York"));
echo "Start: ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;
$dt = $dt->modify("last day of next month");
echo "End:   ", $dt->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P"), PHP_EOL;

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Representation of date and time.
This class behaves the same as DateTimeImmutable, except objects are modified itself when modification methods such as DateTime::modify are called.

warning.para: Calling methods on objects of the class DateTime will change the information encapsulated in these objects, if you want to prevent that you will have to use clone operator to create a new object. Use DateTimeImmutable instead of DateTime to obtain this recommended behaviour by default.

The DateTime constructor now includes the current microseconds in the constructed value. Before this, it would always initialise the microseconds to 0.

A DateTimeZone object representing the timezone of datetime.
If timezone is omitted or null, the current timezone will be used.

note.simpara: The timezone parameter and the current timezone are ignored when the datetime parameter either is a UNIX timestamp (e.g. @946684800) or specifies a timezone (e.g. 2010-01-28T15:00:00+02:00, or 2010-07-05T06:00:00Z).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable instance.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: If an invalid Date/Time string is passed, DateMalformedStringException is thrown. Previous to PHP 8.3, this was Exception.

row.entry: Now throws DateMalformedStringException if an invalid string is passed, instead of Exception.
From now on microseconds are filled with actual value. Not with '00000'.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::__construct example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
try {
    $date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-01');
} catch (Exception $e) {
    echo $e->getMessage();
    exit(1);
}

echo $date->format('Y-m-d');
example.para: Procedural style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = date_create('2000-01-01');
if (!$date) {
    $e = date_get_last_errors();
    foreach ($e['errors'] as $error) {
        echo "$error\n";
    }
    exit(1);
}

echo date_format($date, 'Y-m-d');

example.title: Intricacies of DateTimeImmutable::__construct
example.programlisting:
<?php
date_default_timezone_set('America/Jamaica');

// Specified date/time in PHP's default time zone.
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-01');
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:sP') . "\n";

// Specified date/time in the specified time zone.
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-01', new DateTimeZone('Pacific/Nauru'));
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:sP') . "\n";

// Current date/time in your PHP's default time zone.
$date = new DateTimeImmutable();
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:sP') . "\n";

// Current date/time in the specified time zone.
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('now', new DateTimeZone('Pacific/Nauru'));
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:sP') . "\n";

// Using a UNIX timestamp.  Notice the result is in the UTC time zone.
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('@946684800');
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:sP') . "\n";

// Non-existent values roll over.
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-02-30');
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:sP') . "\n";
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:

note.para: Rolled over dates can be detected by checking for warnings using DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors.

example.title: Changing the associated timezone
example.programlisting:
<?php
$timeZone = new \DateTimeZone('Asia/Tokyo');

$time = new \DateTimeImmutable();
$time = $time->setTimezone($timeZone);

echo $time->format('Y/m/d H:i:s e'), "\n";
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:

example.title: Using a relative date/time string
example.programlisting:
<?php
$time = new \DateTimeImmutable("-1 year");

echo $time->format('Y/m/d H:i:s'), "\n";
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:

refnamediv.refpurpose: Parses a time string according to a specified format

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Object-oriented style
Procedural style
Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object representing the date and time specified by the datetime string, which was formatted in the given format.

listitem.para: The format that the passed in string should be in. See the formatting options below. In most cases, the same letters as for the date can be used.

All fields are initialised with the current date/time. In most cases you would want to reset these to "zero" (the Unix epoch, 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC). You do that by including the ! character as first character in your format, or | as your last. Please see the documentation for each character below for more information.

The format is parsed from left to right, which means that in some situations the order in which the format characters are present affects the result. In the case of z (the day of the year), it is required that a year has already been parsed, for example through the Y or y characters.

Letters that are used for parsing numbers allow a wide range of values, outside of what the logical range would be. For example, the d (day of the month) accepts values in the range from 00 to 99. The only constraint is on the amount of digits. The date/time parser's overflow mechanism is used when out-of-range values are given. The examples below show some of this behaviour.

This also means that the data parsed for a format letter is greedy, and will read up to the amount of digits its format allows for. That can then also mean that there are no longer enough characters in the datetime string for following format characters. An example on this page also illustrates this issue.

table.title: The following characters are recognized in the format parameter string

row.entry: Day of the month, 2 digits with or without leading zeros
01 to 31 or 1 to 31. (2 digit numbers higher than the number of days in the month are accepted, in which case they will make the month overflow. For example using 33 with January, means February 2nd)
A textual representation of a day

Mon through Sun or Sunday through Saturday. If the day name given is different than the day name belonging to a parsed (or default) date is different, then an overflow occurs to the next date with the given day name. See the examples below for an explanation.
English ordinal suffix for the day of the month, 2 characters. It's ignored while processing.
The day of the year (starting from 0); must be preceded by Y or y.
0 through 365. (3 digit numbers higher than the numbers in a year are accepted, in which case they will make the year overflow. For example using 366 with 2022, means January 2nd, 2023)
A textual representation of a month, such as January or Sept
January through December or Jan through Dec
Numeric representation of a month, with or without leading zeros
01 through 12 or 1 through 12. (2 digit numbers higher than 12 are accepted, in which case they will make the year overflow. For example using 13 means January in the next year)
A full numeric representation of a year, up to 19 digits, optionally prefixed by + or -
A full numeric representation of a year, up to 4 digits
A two digit representation of a year (which is assumed to be in the range 1970-2069, inclusive)
Examples: 99 or 03 (which will be interpreted as 1999 and 2003, respectively)
12-hour format of an hour with or without leading zero
1 through 12 or 01 through 12 (2 digit numbers higher than 12 are accepted, in which case they will make the day overflow. For example using 14 means 02 in the next AM/PM period)
24-hour format of an hour with or without leading zeros
0 through 23 or 00 through 23 (2 digit numbers higher than 24 are accepted, in which case they will make the day overflow. For example using 26 means 02:00 the next day)
00 to 59. (2 digit numbers higher than 59 are accepted, in which case they will make the hour overflow. For example using 66 means :06 the next hour)
00 through 59 (2 digit numbers higher than 59 are accepted, in which case they will make the minute overflow. For example using 90 means :30 the next minute)
Fraction in milliseconds (up to three digits)
Fraction in microseconds (up to six digits)
e, O, p, P and T
Timezone identifier, or difference to UTC in hours, or difference to UTC with colon between hours and minutes, or timezone abbreviation
Examples: UTC, GMT, Atlantic/Azores or +0200 or +02:00 or EST, MDT
Seconds since the Unix Epoch (January 1 1970 00:00:00 GMT)
Zero or more spaces, tabs, NBSP (U+A0), or NNBSP (U+202F) characters
One of the following separation symbol: ;, :, /, ., ,, -, ( or )
Example: ^ (Be aware that for UTF-8 characters you might need more than one ?. In this case, using * is probably what you want instead)
Random bytes until the next separator or digit
Example: * in Y-*-d with the string 2009-aWord-08 will match aWord

Resets all fields (year, month, day, hour, minute, second, fraction and timezone information) to zero-like values ( 0 for hour, minute, second and fraction, 1 for month and day, 1970 for year and the default timezone)
Without !, all fields will be set to the current date and time.
Resets all fields (year, month, day, hour, minute, second, fraction and timezone information) to zero-like values if they have not been parsed yet
Y-m-d| will set the year, month and day to the information found in the string to parse, and sets the hour, minute and second to 0.
If this format specifier is present, trailing data in the string will not cause an error, but a warning instead
Use DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors to find out whether trailing data was present.

listitem.para: Unrecognized characters in the format string will cause the parsing to fail and an error message is appended to the returned structure. You can query error messages with DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors.
To include literal characters in format, you have to escape them with a backslash (\).
If format does not contain the character ! then portions of the generated date/time which are not specified in format will be set to the current system time.

If format contains the character !, then portions of the generated date/time not provided in format, as well as values to the left-hand side of the !, will be set to corresponding values from the Unix epoch.
If any time character is parsed, then all other time-related fields are set to "0", unless also parsed.
The Unix epoch is 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.
String representing the time.
A DateTimeZone object representing the desired time zone.
If timezone is omitted or null and datetime contains no timezone, the current timezone will be used.

note.para: The timezone parameter and the current timezone are ignored when the datetime parameter either contains a UNIX timestamp (e.g. 946684800) or specifies a timezone (e.g. 2010-01-28T15:00:00+02:00).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable instance or false on failure.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: This method throws ValueError when the datetime contains NULL-bytes.

row.entry: The (space) specifier now also supports NBSP (U+A0) and NNBSP (U+202F) characters.
The X and x format specifiers have been added.
Now throws ValueError when NULL-bytes are passed into datetime, which previously was silently ignored.
The v format specifier has been added.

refsect1.title: Examples

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('j-M-Y', '15-Feb-2009');
echo $date->format('Y-m-d');

example.title: Using predefined format constants with DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat(
    DateTimeInterface::ISO8601,
    '2004-02-12T15:19:21+00:00'
);
echo $date->format('c e') . "\n";

$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat(
    DateTimeInterface::RFC3339_EXTENDED,
    '2013-10-14T09:00:00.000+02:00'
);
echo $date->format('c e') . "\n";
example.para: The formatting constants as used in this example consist of a string of characters for formatting a DateTimeImmutable object. In most cases, these letters match with the same elements of date/time information as the ones defined in the parameters section above, but they tend to be more lenient.

example.title: Intricacies of DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo 'Current time: ' . date('Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

$format = 'Y-m-d';
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat($format, '2009-02-15');
echo "Format: $format; " . $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

$format = 'Y-m-d H:i:s';
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat($format, '2009-02-15 15:16:17');
echo "Format: $format; " . $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

$format = 'Y-m-!d H:i:s';
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat($format, '2009-02-15 15:16:17');
echo "Format: $format; " . $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

$format = '!d';
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat($format, '15');
echo "Format: $format; " . $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

$format = 'i';
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat($format, '15');
echo "Format: $format; " . $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:

example.title: Format string with literal characters
example.programlisting: <?php echo DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('H\h i\m s\s','23h 15m 03s')->format('H:i:s');
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:

example.title: Overflow behaviour
example.programlisting: <?php echo DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('Y-m-d H:i:s', '2021-17-35 16:60:97')->format(DateTimeImmutable::RFC2822);
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:
example.para: Although the result looks odd, it is correct, as the following overflows happen:

listitem.simpara: 97 seconds overflows to 1 minute, leaving 37 seconds.
61 minutes overflows to 1 hour, leaving 1 minutes.
35 days overflows to 1 month, leaving 4 days. The amount of days that are left over depends on the month, as not every month has the same amount of days.
18 months overflows to 1 year, leaving 6 months.

example.title: Overflowing day name behaviour
example.programlisting:
<?php
$d = DateTime::createFromFormat(DateTimeInterface::RFC1123, 'Mon, 3 Aug 2020 25:00:00 +0000');
echo $d->format(DateTime::RFC1123), "\n";
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:
example.para: Although the result looks odd, it is correct, as the following overflows happen:

listitem.simpara: 3 Aug 2020 25:00:00 overflows to (Tue) 4 Aug 2020 01:00.
Mon gets applied, which advances the date to Mon, 10 Aug 2020 01:00:00. The explanation of relative keywords such as Mon is explained in the section on relative formats.

refsect1.para: In order to detect overflows in dates, you can use DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors, which will include a warning if an overflow occurred.

example.title: Detecting overflown dates
example.programlisting:
<?php
$d = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('Y-m-d H:i:s', '2021-17-35 16:60:97');
echo $d->format(DateTimeImmutable::RFC2822), "\n\n";

var_dump(DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors());
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:

example.title: Greedy parsing behaviour
example.programlisting: <?php print_r(date_parse_from_format('Gis', '60101'));
example.simpara: The above example will output something similar to:
example.screen:
Array ( [year] => [month] => [day] => [hour] => 60 [minute] => 10 [second] => 0 [fraction] => 0 [warning_count] => 1 [warnings] => Array ( [5] => The parsed time was invalid )
[error_count] => 1 [errors] => Array ( [4] => A two digit second could not be found )
[is_localtime] => )
example.para: The G format is to parse 24 hour clock hours, with or without leading zero. This requires to parse 1 or 2 digits. Because there are two following digits, it greedily reads this as 60.
The following i and s format characters both require two digits. This means that 10 is passed as minute (i), and that there are then not enough digits left to parse for as second (s).
The errors array indicates this problem.
Additionally, an hour of 60 is outside the range 0-24, which causes the warnings array to include a warning that the time is invalid.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns new DateTimeImmutable object encapsulating the given DateTimeInterface object

listitem.para: The DateTimeInterface object that needs to be converted to an immutable version. This object is not modified, but instead a new DateTimeImmutable object is created containing the same date, time, and timezone information.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable instance.

example.title: Creating an immutable date time object
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTime("2014-06-20 11:45 Europe/London");
$immutable = DateTimeImmutable::createFromInterface($date);

$date = new DateTimeImmutable("2014-06-20 11:45 Europe/London");
$also_immutable = DateTimeImmutable::createFromInterface($date);

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns new DateTimeImmutable instance encapsulating the given DateTime object

listitem.para: The mutable DateTime object that you want to convert to an immutable version. This object is not modified, but instead a new DateTimeImmutable instance is created containing the same date time and timezone information.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable instance.

row.entry: The method returns an instance of the currently invoked class now. Previously, it created a new instance of DateTimeImmutable.

example.title: Creating an immutable date time object
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTime("2014-06-20 11:45 Europe/London");
$immutable = DateTimeImmutable::createFromMutable( $date );

refnamediv.refpurpose: Creates an instance from a Unix timestamp

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Creates an instance from a Unix timestamp.

listitem.simpara: Unix timestamp representing the date. A float value is also accepted which allows for microsecond precision.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable instance.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.simpara: If the timestamp is outside the range [PHP_INT_MIN, PHP_INT_MAX], a DateRangeError is thrown.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::createFromTimestamp example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromTimestamp(123.456789);
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:s.u');
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns the warnings and errors

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns an array of warnings and errors found while parsing a date/time string.

refsect1.title: Parameters
refsect1.simpara: This function has no parameters.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns array containing info about warnings and errors, or false if there are neither warnings nor errors.

row.entry: Before PHP 8.2.0, this function did not return false when there were no warnings or errors. Instead, it would always return the documented array structure.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors example
example.programlisting:
<?php
try {
    $date = new DateTimeImmutable('asdfasdf');
} catch (Exception $e) {
    // For demonstration purposes only...
    print_r(DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors());

    // The real object-oriented way to do this is
    echo $e->getMessage();
}
?>
example.screen:
Array ( [warning_count] => 1 [warnings] => Array ( [6] => Double timezone specification )
[error_count] => 1 [errors] => Array ( [0] => The timezone could not be found in the database ) ) Failed to parse time string (asdfasdf) at position 0 (a): The timezone could not be found in the database
example.para: The indexes 6, and 0 in the example output refer to the character index in the string where the error occurred.

example.title: Detecting rolled over dates
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('!Y-m-d', '2020-02-30');
print_r(DateTimeImmutable::getLastErrors());
example.screen:
Array ( [warning_count] => 1 [warnings] => Array ( [10] => The parsed date was invalid )
[error_count] => 0 [errors] => Array ( ) )

refnamediv.refpurpose: Creates a new object with modified timestamp

refsect1.title: Description

methodsynopsis.modifier: #[\NoDiscard(message: "as DateTimeImmutable::modify() does not modify the object itself")]

refsect1.para: Creates a new DateTimeImmutable object with modified timestamp. The original object is not modified.

listitem.para: A date/time string. Valid formats are explained in Date and Time Formats.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns DateTimeImmutable on success. Procedural style returns false on failure.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: If an invalid Date/Time string is passed, DateMalformedStringException is thrown. Previous to PHP 8.3, this was a warning.

row.entry: Now has a tentative return type of DateTimeImmutable. Previously it was DateTimeImmutablefalse.
DateTimeImmutable::modify now throws DateMalformedStringException if an invalid string is passed. Previously, it returned false, and a warning was emitted.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::modify example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2006-12-12');
$newDate = $date->modify('+1 day');
echo $newDate->format('Y-m-d');

example.title: Beware when adding or subtracting months
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-12-31');

$newDate1 = $date->modify('+1 month');
echo $newDate1->format('Y-m-d') . "\n";

$newDate2 = $newDate1->modify('+1 month');
echo $newDate2->format('Y-m-d') . "\n";

refnamediv.refpurpose: The __set_state handler

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: The __set_state() handler.

listitem.para: Initialization array.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new instance of a DateTimeImmutable object.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Sets the date

refsect1.title: Description

methodsynopsis.modifier: #[\NoDiscard(message: "as DateTimeImmutable::setDate() does not modify the object itself")]

refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object with the current date of the DateTimeImmutable object set to the given date.

listitem.simpara: Procedural style only: A DateTime object returned by date_create. The function modifies this object.

listitem.para: Year of the date.
Month of the date.
Day of the date.

example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:

example.programlisting:

$date = new DateTimeImmutable();

$newDate = $date->setDate(2001, 2, 28);

$newDate = $date->setDate(2001, 2, 29);

methodsynopsis.modifier: #[\NoDiscard(message: "as DateTimeImmutable::setISODate() does not modify the object itself")]

refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object with the date set according to the ISO 8601 standard - using weeks and day offsets rather than specific dates.

listitem.para: Year of the date.
Week of the date.
Offset from the first day of the week.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object with the modified data.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::setISODate example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:

$date = new DateTimeImmutable();

$newDate = $date->setISODate(2008, 2);

date_isodate_set($date, 2008, 2);

date_isodate_set($date, 2008, 2, 7);

$date = new DateTimeImmutable();

$newDate = $date->setISODate(2008, 2, 7);

methodsynopsis.modifier: #[\NoDiscard(message: "as DateTimeImmutable::setMicrosecond() does not modify the object itself")]

listitem.simpara: The microsecond value to set (0 to 999999).

refsect1.title: Return Values

refnamediv.refpurpose: Sets the date and time based on a Unix timestamp

refsect1.title: Description

methodsynopsis.modifier: #[\NoDiscard(message: "as DateTimeImmutable::setTimestamp() does not modify the object itself")]

refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object constructed from the old one, with the date and time set based on an Unix timestamp.

listitem.para: Unix timestamp representing the date. Setting timestamps outside the range of int is possible by using DateTimeImmutable::modify with the @ format.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object with the modified data.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::setTimestamp example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTimeImmutable();
echo $date->format('U = Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

$newDate = $date->setTimestamp(1171502725);
echo $newDate->format('U = Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

refnamediv.refpurpose: Sets the time zone

refsect1.title: Description

methodsynopsis.modifier: #[\NoDiscard(message: "as DateTimeImmutable::setTimezone() does not modify the object itself")]

refsect1.simpara: Returns a new modified DateTimeImmutable object for method chaining. The underlying point-in-time is not changed when calling this method.

example.programlisting:

$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-01', new DateTimeZone('Pacific/Nauru'));

refnamediv.refpurpose: Subtracts an amount of days, months, years, hours, minutes and seconds

refsect1.title: Description

methodsynopsis.modifier: #[\NoDiscard(message: "as DateTimeImmutable::sub() does not modify the object itself")]

refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object, with the specified DateInterval object subtracted from the specified DateTimeImmutable object.

listitem.para: A DateInterval object

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a new DateTimeImmutable object with the modified data.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: If an unsupported operation is attempted, such as using a DateInterval object representing relative time specifications such as next weekday, a DateInvalidOperationException is thrown.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::sub example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-20');
$newDate = $date->sub(new DateInterval('P10D'));
echo $newDate->format('Y-m-d') . "\n";
?>

example.title: Further DateTimeImmutable::sub examples
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-20');
$newDate = $date->sub(new DateInterval('PT10H30S'));
echo $newDate->format('Y-m-d H:i:s') . "\n";

$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-20');
$newDate = $date->sub(new DateInterval('P7Y5M4DT4H3M2S'));

?>

example.title: Beware when subtracting months
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2001-04-30');
$interval = new DateInterval('P1M');

$newDate1 = $date->sub($interval);
echo $newDate1->format('Y-m-d') . "\n";

$newDate2 = $newDate1->sub($interval);
echo $newDate2->format('Y-m-d') . "\n";

section.title: Introduction
section.para: DateTimeInterface was created so that parameter, return, or property type declarations may accept either DateTimeImmutable or DateTime as a value. It is not possible to implement this interface with userland classes.
Common constants that allow for formatting DateTimeImmutable or DateTime objects through DateTimeImmutable::format and DateTime::format are also defined on this interface.

listitem.simpara: Atom (example: 2005-08-15T15:52:01+00:00); compatible with ISO-8601, RFC 3339, and XML Schema
HTTP Cookies (example: Monday, 15-Aug-2005 15:52:01 UTC)

note.simpara: This format is not compatible with ISO-8601, but is left this way for backward compatibility reasons. Use DateTimeInterface::ISO8601_EXPANDED, DateTimeInterface::ATOM for compatibility with ISO-8601 instead. (ref ISO8601:2004 section 4.3.3 clause d)
This format allows for year ranges outside of ISO-8601's normal range of 0000-9999 by always including a sign character. It also ensures that the timezone part (+01:00) is compatible with ISO-8601.

listitem.simpara: RFC 822 (example: Mon, 15 Aug 05 15:52:01 +0000)
RFC 850 (example: Monday, 15-Aug-05 15:52:01 UTC)
RFC 7231 (since PHP 7.0.19 and 7.1.5) (example: Sat, 30 Apr 2016 17:52:13 GMT)
Same as DATE_ATOM
RFC 3339 EXTENDED format (example: 2005-08-15T15:52:01.000+00:00)
RSS (example: Mon, 15 Aug 2005 15:52:01 +0000)
World Wide Web Consortium (example: 2005-08-15T15:52:01+00:00)

row.entry: The DATE_RFC7231 and DateTimeInterface::RFC7231 constants have been deprecated.
The class constants are now typed.
The class constants of DateTime are now defined on DateTimeInterface.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns the difference between two DateTime objects

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Object-oriented style
Procedural style
Returns the difference between two DateTimeInterface objects.

listitem.para: The date to compare to.
Should the interval be forced to be positive?

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The DateInterval object represents the difference between the two dates.
The absolute parameter only affects the invert property of a DateInterval object.
The return value more specifically represents the clock-time interval to apply to the original object ($this or $originObject) to arrive at the $targetObject. This process is not always reversible.

The method is aware of DST changeovers, and hence can return an interval of 24 hours and 30 minutes, as per one of the examples. If you want to calculate with absolute time, you need to convert both the $this/$baseObject, and $targetObject to UTC first.

example.title: DateTimeImmutable::diff example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$origin = new DateTimeImmutable('2009-10-11');
$target = new DateTimeImmutable('2009-10-13');
$interval = $origin->diff($target);
echo $interval->format('%R%a days');
example.para: Procedural style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$origin = date_create('2009-10-11');
$target = date_create('2009-10-13');
$interval = date_diff($origin, $target);
echo $interval->format('%R%a days');

example.title: DateTimeInterface::diff during DST changeover
example.programlisting:
<?php
$originalTime = new DateTimeImmutable("2021-10-30 09:00:00 Europe/London");
$targetTime = new DateTimeImmutable("2021-10-31 08:30:00 Europe/London");
$interval = $originalTime->diff($targetTime);
echo $interval->format("%H:%I:%S (Full days: %a)"), "\n";

example.title: DateTimeInterface::diff range
example.para: The value that the method returns is the exact amount of time to get from $this to $targetObject. Comparing January 1st to December 31st returns therefore 364, and not 365, days (for non-leap years).
example.programlisting:
<?php
$originalTime = new DateTimeImmutable("2023-01-01 UTC");
$targetTime = new DateTimeImmutable("2023-12-31 UTC");
$interval = $originalTime->diff($targetTime);
echo "Full days: ", $interval->format("%a"), "\n";

example.title: DateTime object comparison

note.para: DateTimeImmutable and DateTime objects can be compared using comparison operators.

example.programlisting:
<?php
$date1 = new DateTime("now");
$date2 = new DateTime("tomorrow");

var_dump($date1 == $date2);
var_dump($date1 < $date2);
var_dump($date1 > $date2);

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns date formatted according to given format

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Object-oriented style
Procedural style
Returns date formatted according to given format.

listitem.simpara: Procedural style only: A DateTime object returned by date_create

listitem.para: The format of the outputted date string. See the formatting options below. There are also several predefined date constants that may be used instead, so for example DATE_RSS contains the format string 'D, d M Y H:i:s'.

table.title: The following characters are recognized in the format parameter string

row.entry: Day of the month, 2 digits with leading zeros
A textual representation of a day, three letters
Day of the month without leading zeros
A full textual representation of the day of the week
ISO 8601 numeric representation of the day of the week
English ordinal suffix for the day of the month, 2 characters
st, nd, rd or th. Works well with j
Numeric representation of the day of the week
The day of the year (starting from 0)
ISO 8601 week number of year, weeks starting on Monday
A full textual representation of a month, such as January or March
Numeric representation of a month, with leading zeros
A short textual representation of a month, three letters
Numeric representation of a month, without leading zeros
Number of days in the given month
1 if it is a leap year, 0 otherwise.
ISO 8601 week-numbering year. This has the same value as Y, except that if the ISO week number (W) belongs to the previous or next year, that year is used instead.
An expanded full numeric representation of a year, at least 4 digits, with - for years BCE, and + for years CE.

An expanded full numeric representation if required, or a standard full numeral representation if possible (like Y). At least four digits. Years BCE are prefixed with a -. Years beyond (and including) 10000 are prefixed by a +.
A full numeric representation of a year, at least 4 digits, with - for years BCE.
A two digit representation of a year
Lowercase Ante meridiem and Post meridiem
Uppercase Ante meridiem and Post meridiem
12-hour format of an hour without leading zeros
24-hour format of an hour without leading zeros
12-hour format of an hour with leading zeros
24-hour format of an hour with leading zeros

Microseconds. Note that date will always generate 000000 since it takes an int parameter, whereas DateTimeInterface::format does support microseconds if an object of type DateTimeInterface was created with microseconds.
Milliseconds. Same note applies as for u.
Whether or not the date is in daylight saving time
Difference to Greenwich time (GMT) without colon between hours and minutes
Difference to Greenwich time (GMT) with colon between hours and minutes
The same as P, but returns Z instead of +00:00 (available as of PHP 8.0.0)
Timezone abbreviation, if known; otherwise the GMT offset.
Timezone offset in seconds. The offset for timezones west of UTC is always negative, and for those east of UTC is always positive.
ISO 8601 date. Only compatible with the non-expanded format (up to year 9999). Later dates will result in an invalid string. For later dates and expanded format, see x and X.
Seconds since the Unix Epoch (January 1 1970 00:00:00 GMT)

listitem.para: Unrecognized characters in the format string will be printed as-is. The Z format will always return 0 when using gmdate.

note.para: Since this function only accepts int timestamps the u format character is only useful when using the date_format function with user based timestamps created with date_create.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns the formatted date string on success.

row.entry: The format characters X and x have been added.
The format character p has been added.

refsect1.title: Examples

example.title: DateTimeInterface::format example
example.para: Object-oriented style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = new DateTimeImmutable('2000-01-01');
echo $date->format('Y-m-d H:i:s');
?>
example.para: Procedural style
example.programlisting:
<?php
$date = date_create('2000-01-01');
echo date_format($date, 'Y-m-d H:i:s');
?>

example.title: More examples
example.programlisting:
<?php
// set the default timezone to use.
date_default_timezone_set('UTC');

// now
$date = new DateTimeImmutable();

// Prints something like: Wednesday
echo $date->format('l'), "\n";

// Prints something like: Wednesday 19th of October 2022 08:40:48 AM
echo $date->format('l jS \o\f F Y h:i:s A'), "\n";

/* use the constants in the format parameter */
// prints something like: Wed, 19 Oct 2022 08:40:48 +0000
echo $date->format(DateTimeInterface::RFC2822), "\n";
?>

refsect1.para: To format dates in other languages, IntlDateFormatter::format can be used instead of DateTimeInterface::format.

refsect1.title: Notes
refsect1.para: This method does not use locales. All output is in English.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Serialize a DateTime

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: The __serialize() handler.

refsect1.title: Parameters
refsect1.simpara: This function has no parameters.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The serialized representation of the DateTime object.

example.title: DateTime::__serialize example
example.programlisting:
<?php

class CustomDateTimeImmutable extends DateTimeImmutable
{
    #[\Override]
    public function __serialize(): array
    {
        return [
            'date' => $this->format(DateTimeInterface::W3C),
            'timestamp' => $this->getTimestamp(),
            'timezone' => $this->getTimeZone()->getName(),
            'to' => 'Drink a cup of coffee',
        ];
    }
}

$date = new CustomDateTimeImmutable('2025-03-27');
var_dump(serialize($date));

warning.simpara: An Error is thrown when attempting to unserialize a custom DateTime object if __serialize() is defined but __unserialize() is missing.

refsect1.para: The __unserialize() handler.

listitem.para: The serialized DateTime.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: No value is returned.

example.title: DateTime::__unserialize example
example.programlisting:
<?php

class CustomDateTimeImmutable extends DateTimeImmutable
{
    #[\Override]
    public function __unserialize(array $data): void
    {
        echo "Time to `{$data['to']}`:\n\n";

        parent::__construct($data['date'], new DateTimeZone($data['timezone']));
    }
}

$serializedData = 'O:23:"CustomDateTimeImmutable":4:{s:4:"date";s:25:"2025-03-27T00:00:00+00:00";s:9:"timestamp";i:1743033600;s:8:"timezone";s:3:"UTC";s:2:"to";s:21:"Drink a cup of coffee";}';

var_dump(unserialize($serializedData));

refnamediv.refpurpose: Creates new DateTimeZone object

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Object-oriented style
Procedural style
Creates a new DateTimeZone object.

A DateTimeZone object provides access to three different types of timezone rules: UTC offset (type 1), timezone abbreviation (type 2), and timezone identifiers as published in the IANA timezone database (type 3).
The DateTimeZone object can be attached to DateTime and DateTimeImmutable objects to be able to render the timezone encapsulated by these objects in a local timezone.

listitem.para: One of the supported timezone names, an offset value (+0200), or a timezone abbreviation (BST).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns DateTimeZone on success. Procedural style returns false on failure.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: This method throws DateInvalidTimeZoneException if the timezone supplied is not recognised as a valid timezone. Prior to PHP 8.3, this was an Exception instead.

row.entry: Invalid values now return a DateInvalidTimeZoneException instead of a generic Exception.

example.title: Creating and attaching DateTimeZone to a DateTimeImmutable
example.programlisting:
<?php
$d = new DateTimeImmutable("2022-06-02 15:44:48 UTC");

$timezones = [ 'Europe/London', 'GMT+04:45', '-06:00', 'CEST' ];

foreach ($timezones as $tz) {
    $tzo = new DateTimeZone($tz);

    $local = $d->setTimezone($tzo);
    echo $local->format(DateTimeInterface::RFC2822 . ' — e') . "\n";
}

example.title: Catching errors when instantiating DateTimeZone
example.programlisting:
<?php
// Error handling by catching exceptions
$timezones = array('Europe/London', 'Mars/Phobos', 'Jupiter/Europa');

foreach ($timezones as $tz) {
    try {
        $mars = new DateTimeZone($tz);
        echo $mars->getName() . "\n";
    } catch(Exception $e) {
        echo $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    }
}
example.screen: Europe/London DateTimeZone::__construct() [datetimezone.--construct]: Unknown or bad timezone (Mars/Phobos) DateTimeZone::__construct() [datetimezone.--construct]: Unknown or bad timezone (Jupiter/Europa)

refsect1.para: The country_code elements contains the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code for each entry. The latitude and longitude elements the coordinates of the named city from the time zone identifier, and comments contain (when not false) a hint of where in the given country this timezone applies. This information is suitable to present to end-users.

Returns the name of the timezone.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Depending on zone type, UTC offset (type 1), timezone abbreviation (type 2), and timezone identifiers as published in the IANA timezone database (type 3), the descriptor string to create a new DateTimeZone object with the same offset and/or rules. For example 02:00, CEST, or one of the timezone names in the list of timezones.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns the timezone offset from GMT

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Object-oriented style
Procedural style

This function returns the offset to GMT for the date/time specified in the datetime parameter. The GMT offset is calculated with the timezone information contained in the DateTimeZone object being used.

listitem.simpara: Procedural style only: A DateTimeZone object returned by timezone_open

listitem.para: DateTime that contains the date/time to compute the offset from.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns time zone offset in seconds.

example.title: DateTimeZone::getOffset examples
example.programlisting:
<?php
// Create two timezone objects, one for Taipei (Taiwan) and one for
// Tokyo (Japan)
$dateTimeZoneTaipei = new DateTimeZone("Asia/Taipei");
$dateTimeZoneJapan = new DateTimeZone("Asia/Tokyo");

// Create two DateTime objects that will contain the same Unix timestamp, but
// have different timezones attached to them.
$dateTimeTaipei = new DateTime("now", $dateTimeZoneTaipei);
$dateTimeJapan = new DateTime("now", $dateTimeZoneJapan);

// Calculate the GMT offset for the date/time contained in the $dateTimeTaipei
// object, but using the timezone rules as defined for Tokyo
// ($dateTimeZoneJapan).
$timeOffset = $dateTimeZoneJapan->getOffset($dateTimeTaipei);

// Should show int(32400) (for dates after Sat Sep 8 01:00:00 1951 JST).
var_dump($timeOffset);

If timestampBegin is given, the first entry in the returned array will contain a transition element at the time of timestampBegin.

row.entry: DateTimeInterface::ISO8601_EXPANDED (PHP 8.2 and later), or DateTimeInterface::ISO8601 (PHP 8.1 and lower) time string
Whether daylight saving time is active
The default value of timestampEnd has been changed to 2147483647. Previously, it was PHP_INT_MAX.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns associative array containing dst, offset and the timezone name

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Object-oriented style
Procedural style

The returned list of abbreviations includes all historical use of abbreviations, which can lead to correct, but confusing entries. There are also conflicts, as PST is used both in the US and in the Philippines.
The list that this function returns is therefore not suitable for building an array with options to present a choice of timezone to users.

note.para: The data for this function are precompiled for performance reasons, and are not updated when using a newer timezonedb.

refsect1.simpara: This function has no parameters.

refsect1.title: Return Values

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Represents a date interval.
A date interval stores either a fixed amount of time (in years, months, days, hours etc) or a relative time string in the format that DateTimeImmutable's and DateTime's constructors support.
More specifically, the information in an object of the DateInterval class is an instruction to get from one date/time to another date/time. This process is not always reversible.
A common way to create a DateInterval object is by calculating the difference between two date/time objects through DateTimeInterface::diff.
section.simpara: How the time part of an interval, that is hours, minutes, seconds and microseconds, is applied when the interval is added to, or subtracted from, a date/time object depends on how the interval was created. For an interval created with DateInterval::__construct the time part covers elapsed time, whereas for an interval created with DateInterval::createFromDateString, or returned by DateTimeInterface::diff, it increments or decrements the individual component values. The date part, that is years, months and days, always increments or decrements the individual component values. The two therefore only give a different result when a timezone transition falls within the time part of the interval; see Date/Time Arithmetic.
section.para: Since there is no well defined way to compare date intervals, DateInterval instances are incomparable.

warning.para: The available properties listed below depend on PHP version, and should be considered as readonly.

listitem.para: Number of years.
Number of months.
Number of days.
Number of hours.
Number of minutes.
Number of seconds.
Number of microseconds, as a fraction of a second.
Is 1 if the interval represents a negative time period and 0 otherwise. See DateInterval::format.
If the DateInterval object was created by DateTimeImmutable::diff or DateTime::diff, then this is the total number of full days between the start and end dates. Otherwise, days will be false.

If the DateInterval object was created by DateInterval::createFromDateString, then this property's value will be true, and the date_string property will be populated. Otherwise, the value will be false, and the y to f, invert, and days properties will be populated.
The string used as argument to DateInterval::createFromDateString.

row.entry: The from_string and date_string properties were added for DateInterval instances that were created using the DateInterval::createFromDateString method.
Only the y to f, invert, and days will be visible.
DateInterval instances are incomparable now; previously, all DateInterval instances were considered equal.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Creates a new DateInterval object

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Creates a new DateInterval object.

listitem.para: An interval specification.

The format starts with the letter P, for period. Each duration period is represented by an integer value followed by a period designator. If the duration contains time elements, that portion of the specification is preceded by the letter T.

row.entry: weeks. Converted into days. Prior to PHP 8.0.0, can not be combined with D.

listitem.para: Here are some simple examples. Two days is P2D. Two seconds is PT2S. Six years and five minutes is P6YT5M.

note.para: The unit types must be entered from the largest scale unit on the left to the smallest scale unit on the right. So years before months, months before days, days before minutes, etc. Thus one year and four days must be represented as P1Y4D, not P4D1Y.

listitem.para: The specification can also be represented as a date time. A sample of one year and four days would be P0001-00-04T00:00:00. But the values in this format can not exceed a given period's roll-over-point (e.g. 25 hours is invalid).
These formats are based on the ISO 8601 duration specification.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: Throws an DateMalformedIntervalStringException when the duration cannot be parsed as an interval. Prior to PHP 8.3, this was Exception.

row.entry: Now throws DateMalformedIntervalStringException instead of Exception.
Only the y to f, invert, and days will be visible, including a new from_string boolean property.
W can be combined with D.

example.title: Constructing and using DateInterval objects
example.programlisting:
<?php
// Create a specific date
$someDate = \DateTime::createFromFormat("Y-m-d H:i", "2022-08-25 14:18");

// Create interval
$interval = new \DateInterval("P7D");

// Add interval
$someDate->add($interval);

// Convert interval to string
echo $interval->format("%d");

example.title: DateInterval example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$interval = new DateInterval('P1W2D');
var_dump($interval);

refnamediv.refpurpose: Sets up a DateInterval from the relative parts of the string

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Object-oriented style
Procedural style
Uses the date/time parsers as used in the DateTimeImmutable constructor to create a DateInterval from the relative parts of the parsed string.

listitem.simpara: A date with relative parts. Specifically, the relative formats supported by the parser used for DateTimeImmutable, DateTime, and strtotime will be used to construct the DateInterval.
To use an ISO-8601 format string like P7D, you must use the DateInterval::__construct.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns DateInterval on success. Procedural style returns false on failure.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: Object Oriented API only: If an invalid Date/Time string is passed, DateMalformedIntervalStringException is thrown.

row.entry: Now has a tentative return type of DateInterval. Previously it was DateIntervalfalse.

DateInterval::createFromDateString now throws DateMalformedIntervalStringException if an invalid string is passed. Previously, it returned false, and a warning was emitted. date_interval_create_from_date_string has not been changed.
Only the from_string and date_string properties will be visible when a DateInterval is created with this method.

example.title: Parsing valid date intervals
example.programlisting:
<?php
// Each set of intervals describes the same duration.
$i = new DateInterval('P1D');
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('1 day');

$i = new DateInterval('P2W');
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('2 weeks');

$i = new DateInterval('P3M');
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('3 months');

$i = new DateInterval('P4Y');
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('4 years');

$i = new DateInterval('P1Y1D');
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('1 year + 1 day');

$i = new DateInterval('P1DT12H');
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('1 day + 12 hours');

$i = new DateInterval('PT3600S');
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('3600 seconds');

note.simpara: The intervals in a set that have a time part, such as P1DT12H and 1 day + 12 hours, are not interchangeable when they are added to a date/time object and a timezone transition falls within that time part: for an interval created with DateInterval::__construct the time part covers elapsed time, whereas for an interval created with this method it increments or decrements the individual component values. See Date/Time Arithmetic.

example.title: Parsing combinations and negative intervals
example.programlisting:
<?php
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('62 weeks + 1 day + 2 weeks + 2 hours + 70 minutes');
echo $i->format('%d %h %i'), "\n";

$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('1 year - 10 days');
echo $i->format('%y %d'), "\n";

example.title: Parsing special relative date intervals
example.programlisting:
<?php
$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('last day of next month');
var_dump($i);

$i = DateInterval::createFromDateString('last weekday');
var_dump($i);
