refnamediv.refpurpose: Set or get default scale parameter for all bc math functions

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Sets the default scale parameter for all subsequent calls to bc math functions that do not explicitly specify a scale parameter.
Gets the current scale factor.

listitem.para: The scale factor.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns the old scale when used as setter. Otherwise the current scale is returned.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.simpara: This function throws a ValueError if scale is outside the valid range.

row.entry: bcscale can now be used to get the current scale factor; when used as setter, it now returns the old scale value. Formerly, scale was mandatory, and bcscale always returned true.

example.title: bcscale example
example.programlisting:
<?php

// default scale : 3
bcscale(3);
echo bcdiv('105', '6.55957'); // 16.007

// this is the same without bcscale()
echo bcdiv('105', '6.55957', 3); // 16.007

?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Get the square root of an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Return the square root of num.

listitem.para: The operand, as a well-formed BCMath numeric string.

listitem.simpara: This parameter is used to set the number of digits after the decimal place in the result. If null, it will default to the default scale set with bcscale, or fallback to the value of the bcmath.scale INI directive.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns the square root as a well-formed BCMath numeric string.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This function throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is not a well-formed BCMath numeric string num is less than 0 scale is outside the valid range

row.entry: If num is not a well-formed BCMath numeric string, or less than 0, a ValueError is thrown. Previously, E_WARNING was raised instead.
scale now needs to be between 0 and 2147483647; previously, negative scales have been silently treated as 0.

example.title: bcsqrt example
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo bcsqrt('2', 3); // 1.414
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Subtract one arbitrary precision number from another

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Subtracts num2 from num1.

listitem.para: The left operand, as a string.
The right operand, as a string.

listitem.simpara: This parameter is used to set the number of digits after the decimal place in the result. If null, it will default to the default scale set with bcscale, or fallback to the value of the bcmath.scale INI directive.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The result of the subtraction, as a string.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This function throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num1 or num2 is not a well-formed BCMath numeric string.
scale is outside the valid range.

section.title: Introduction
section.simpara: A class for an arbitrary precision number. These objects support overloaded arithmetic and comparison operators.

note.simpara: This class is not affected by the bcmath.scale INI directive set in php.ini.
The behavior of an overloaded operator is the same as specifying null for the scale parameter on the corresponding method.

listitem.simpara: A string representation of an arbitrary precision number.
The scale value currently set on the object. For objects resulting from calculations, this value is automatically computed and set, unless the scale parameter was set in the calculation method.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Adds an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Adds $this and num.

listitem.simpara: The value to add.
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result of addition as a new BcMath\Number object.
When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, the greater BcMath\Number::scale of the two numbers used for addition is used.
That is, if the BcMath\Number::scales of two values are 2 and 5 respectively, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result will be 5.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string scale is outside the valid range

example.title: BcMath\Number::add example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

$ret1 = $number->add(new BcMath\Number('2.34567'));
$ret2 = $number->add('-3.456');
$ret3 = $number->add(7);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::add example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

$ret1 = $number->add(new BcMath\Number('2.34567'), 1);
$ret2 = $number->add('-3.456', 10);
$ret3 = $number->add(7, 0);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Rounds up an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns the next highest integer value by rounding up $this if necessary.

refsect1.title: Parameters
refsect1.simpara: This function has no parameters.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result as a new BcMath\Number object. The BcMath\Number::scale of the result is always 0.

example.title: BcMath\Number::ceil example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$num1 = new BcMath\Number('4.3')->ceil();
$num2 = new BcMath\Number('9.999')->ceil();
$num3 = new BcMath\Number('-3.14')->ceil();

var_dump($num1, $num2, $num3);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Compares two arbitrary precision numbers

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Compare two arbitrary precision numbers. This method behaves similar to the spaceship operator.

listitem.simpara: The value to be compared to.
Specify the scale to use for comparison. If null, all digits are used in the comparison.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns 0 if the two numbers are equal, 1 if $this is greater than num, -1 otherwise.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string scale is outside the valid range

example.title: BcMath\Number::compare example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

var_dump(
    $number->compare(new BcMath\Number('1.234')),
    $number->compare('1.23400'),
    $number->compare('1.23401'),
    $number->compare(1),
);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::compare example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

var_dump(
    $number->compare(new BcMath\Number('1.299'), 1),
    $number->compare('1.24', 2),
    $number->compare('1.22', 2),
    $number->compare(1, 0),
);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Creates a BcMath\Number object

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Creates a BcMath\Number object from an int or string value.

listitem.simpara: An int or string value. If num is a int, the BcMath\Number::scale is always set to 0. If num is a string, it must be a valid number, and the BcMath\Number::scale is automatically set by parsing the string.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.simpara: This method throws a ValueError if num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string.

example.title: BcMath\Number::__construct example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$num1 = new BcMath\Number(100);
$num2 = new BcMath\Number('-200');
$num3 = new BcMath\Number('300.00');

var_dump($num1, $num2, $num3);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Divides by an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Divides $this by num.

listitem.simpara: The divisor.
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result of division as a new BcMath\Number object.

When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, the BcMath\Number::scale of the dividend is used. However, in cases such as indivisible division, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result is expanded. Expansion is done only as needed, up to a maximum of +10.
That is, if the BcMath\Number::scale of the dividend is 5, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result is between 5 and 15.

Even in indivisible calculations, the BcMath\Number::scale will not always be +10. A 0 at the end of the result is considered not to need expansion, so the BcMath\Number::scale is reduced by that amount. The BcMath\Number::scale will never be less than the BcMath\Number::scale before expansion. See also the code example.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string scale is outside the valid range BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is outside the valid range
refsect1.simpara: This method throws a DivisionByZeroError exception if num is 0.

example.title: BcMath\Number::div example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('0.002');

$ret1 = $number->div(new BcMath\Number('2.000'));
$ret2 = $number->div('-3');
$ret3 = $number->div(32);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::div example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('0.002');

$ret1 = $number->div(new BcMath\Number('2.000'), 15);
$ret2 = $number->div('-3', 5);
$ret3 = $number->div(32, 2);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::div example of expansioning BcMath\Number::scale of result object
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump( new BcMath\Number('0.001')->div('10001'), new BcMath\Number('0.001')->div('10001', 13), new BcMath\Number('0.001')->div('100000000000001'), ); ?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Gets the quotient and modulus of an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Gets the quotient and remainder of dividing $this by num.

listitem.simpara: The divisor.
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns an indexed array where the first element is the quotient as a new BcMath\Number object and the second element is the remainder as a new BcMath\Number object.
The quotient is always an integer value, so BcMath\Number::scale of the quotient will always be 0, regardless of whether explicitly specify scale.

If scale is explicitly specified, BcMath\Number::scale of the remainder will be the specified value. When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result's remainder object is automatically set, the greater BcMath\Number::scale of the two numbers used for modulus operation is used.
That is, if the BcMath\Number::scales of two values are 2 and 5 respectively, the BcMath\Number::scale of the remainder will be 5.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string scale is outside the valid range
refsect1.simpara: This method throws a DivisionByZeroError exception if num is 0.

example.title: BcMath\Number::divmod example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo '8.3 / 2.22' . PHP_EOL;
[$quot, $rem] = new BcMath\Number('8')->divmod(new BcMath\Number('2.22'));
var_dump($quot, $rem);

echo PHP_EOL . '8.3 / 8.3' . PHP_EOL;
[$quot, $rem] = new BcMath\Number('8.3')->divmod('8.3');
var_dump($quot, $rem);

echo PHP_EOL . '10 / -3' . PHP_EOL;
[$quot, $rem] = new BcMath\Number('10')->divmod(-3);
var_dump($quot, $rem);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::divmod example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo '8.3 / 2.22' . PHP_EOL;
[$quot, $rem] = new BcMath\Number('8')->divmod(new BcMath\Number('2.22'), 1);
var_dump($quot, $rem);

echo PHP_EOL . '8.3 / 8.3' . PHP_EOL;
[$quot, $rem] = new BcMath\Number('8.3')->divmod('8.3', 4);
var_dump($quot, $rem);

echo PHP_EOL . '10 / -3' . PHP_EOL;
[$quot, $rem] = new BcMath\Number('10')->divmod(-3, 5);
var_dump($quot, $rem);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Rounds down an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns the next highest integer value by rounding down $this if necessary.

refsect1.title: Parameters
refsect1.simpara: This function has no parameters.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result as a new BcMath\Number object. The BcMath\Number::scale of the result is always 0.

example.title: BcMath\Number::floor example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$num1 = new BcMath\Number('4.3')->floor();
$num2 = new BcMath\Number('9.999')->floor();
$num3 = new BcMath\Number('-3.14')->floor();

var_dump($num1, $num2, $num3);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Gets the modulus of an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Gets the remainder of dividing $this by num. Unless num is 0, the result has the same sign as $this.

listitem.simpara: The divisor.
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the modulus as a new BcMath\Number object.
When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, the greater BcMath\Number::scale of the two numbers used for modulus operation is used.
That is, if the BcMath\Number::scales of two values are 2 and 5 respectively, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result will be 5.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string scale is outside the valid range
refsect1.simpara: This method throws a DivisionByZeroError exception if num is 0.

example.title: BcMath\Number::mod example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('8.3');

$ret1 = $number->mod(new BcMath\Number('2.22'));
$ret2 = $number->mod('8.3');
$ret3 = $number->mod(-5);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::mod example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('8.3');

$ret1 = $number->mod(new BcMath\Number('2.22'), 1);
$ret2 = $number->mod('8.3', 3);
$ret3 = $number->mod(-5, 0);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Multiplies an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Multiplies $this by num.

listitem.simpara: The multiplier.
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result of multiplication as a new BcMath\Number object.
When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, the sum of the BcMath\Number::scales of the two values used for multiplication is used.
That is, if the BcMath\Number::scales of two values are 2 and 5 respectively, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result will be 7.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string scale is outside the valid range BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is outside the valid range

example.title: BcMath\Number::mul example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

$ret1 = $number->mul(new BcMath\Number('2.3456'));
$ret2 = $number->mul('-3.4');
$ret3 = $number->mul(7);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::mul example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

$ret1 = $number->mul(new BcMath\Number('2.3456'), 1);
$ret2 = $number->mul('-3.4', 10);
$ret3 = $number->mul(7, 0);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Raises an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Raises $this to the exponent power.

listitem.simpara: The exponent. Must be a value with no fractional part. The valid range of the exponent is platform specific, but it is at least -2147483648 to 2147483647.
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result of power as a new BcMath\Number object.
refsect1.para:
When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, depending on the value of exponent, the BcMath\Number::scale of result will be as follows:
exponent BcMath\Number::scale of result
positive (BcMath\Number::scale of power base) * (exponent's value)
0 0
negative Between (BcMath\Number::scale of power base) and (BcMath\Number::scale of power base + 10)
refsect1.simpara: If an indivisible division occurs due to a negative exponent, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result is expanded. Expansion is done only as needed, up to a maximum of +10. This behavior is the same as BcMath\Number::div, so please see that for details.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
exponent is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string exponent has a fractional part exponent or scale is outside the valid range BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is outside the valid range
refsect1.simpara: This method throws a DivisionByZeroError exception if $this's value is 0 and exponent is a negative value.

example.title: BcMath\Number::pow example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('3.0');

$ret1 = $number->pow(new BcMath\Number('5'));
$ret2 = $number->pow('-1');
$ret3 = $number->pow(0);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::pow example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('3.0');

$ret1 = $number->pow(new BcMath\Number('5'), 0);
$ret2 = $number->pow('-1', 2);
$ret3 = $number->pow(0, 10);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Raises an arbitrary precision number, reduced by a specified modulus

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Use the fast-exponentiation method to raise $this to the power exponent with respect to the modulus modulus.

listitem.simpara: The exponent, as an non-negative and integral (i.e. the scale has to be zero).
The modulus, as an integral (i.e. the scale has to be zero).
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result as a new BcMath\Number object.
When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object will always be 0.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
exponent or modulus is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string $this, exponent or modulus has a fractional part exponent is a negative value scale is outside the valid range
refsect1.simpara: This method throws a DivisionByZeroError exception if modulus is 0.

example.title: BcMath\Number::powmod example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump( new BcMath\Number('8')->powmod(new BcMath\Number('3'), 5), new BcMath\Number('-8')->powmod(new BcMath\Number('3'), 5), new BcMath\Number('8')->powmod('2', -3), new BcMath\Number('-8')->powmod(5, 7), ); ?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::powmod example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump( new BcMath\Number('8')->powmod(new BcMath\Number('3'), 5, 1), new BcMath\Number('-8')->powmod(new BcMath\Number('3'), 5, 2), new BcMath\Number('8')->powmod('2', -3, 3), new BcMath\Number('-8')->powmod(5, 7, 4), ); ?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Rounds an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns the rounded value of $this to specified precision (number of digits after the decimal point). precision can also be negative or zero (default).

listitem.para: The optional number of decimal digits to round to.
If the precision is positive, num is rounded to precision significant digits after the decimal point.

If the precision is negative, num is rounded to precision significant digits before the decimal point, i.e. to the nearest multiple of pow(10, -$precision), e.g. for a precision of -1 num is rounded to tens, for a precision of -2 to hundreds, etc.

listitem.simpara: Specifies the rounding mode. For more information about modes, see RoundingMode.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result as a new BcMath\Number object.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.simpara: This method throws a ValueError if an invalid mode is specified.

example.title: BcMath\Number::round example
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump( new BcMath\Number('3.4')->round(), new BcMath\Number('3.5')->round(), new BcMath\Number('3.6')->round(), new BcMath\Number('3.6')->round(0), new BcMath\Number('5.045')->round(2), new BcMath\Number('5.055')->round(2), new BcMath\Number('345')->round(-2), new BcMath\Number('345')->round(-3), new BcMath\Number('678')->round(-2), new BcMath\Number('678')->round(-3), ); ?>

example.title: Example of using BcMath\Number::round with different precision values
example.programlisting:
<?php $number = new BcMath\Number('123.45');
var_dump( $number->round(3), $number->round(2), $number->round(1), $number->round(0), $number->round(-1), $number->round(-2), $number->round(-3), ); ?>

example.title: Example of using BcMath\Number::round with different mode values
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo 'Rounding modes with 9.5' . PHP_EOL;
$number = new BcMath\Number('9.5');
var_dump(
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfTowardsZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfEven),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfOdd),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::TowardsZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::AwayFromZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::NegativeInfinity),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Rounding modes with 8.5' . PHP_EOL;
$number = new BcMath\Number('8.5');
var_dump(
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfTowardsZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfEven),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::HalfOdd),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::TowardsZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::AwayFromZero),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::NegativeInfinity),
    $number->round(0, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity),
);
?>

example.title: Example of using BcMath\Number::round with different mode values when specifying precision
example.programlisting:
<?php
$positive = new BcMath\Number('1.55');
$negative = new BcMath\Number('-1.55');

echo 'Using RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(
    $positive->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero),
    $negative->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using RoundingMode::HalfTowardsZero with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(
    $positive->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfTowardsZero),
    $negative->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfTowardsZero),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using RoundingMode::HalfEven with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(
    $positive->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfEven),
    $negative->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfEven),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using RoundingMode::HalfOdd with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(
    $positive->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfOdd),
    $negative->round(1, RoundingMode::HalfOdd),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using RoundingMode::TowardsZero with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(
    $positive->round(1, RoundingMode::TowardsZero),
    $negative->round(1, RoundingMode::TowardsZero),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using RoundingMode::AwayFromZero with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(
    $positive->round(1, RoundingMode::AwayFromZero),
    $negative->round(1, RoundingMode::AwayFromZero),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using RoundingMode::NegativeInfinity with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(
    $positive->round(1, RoundingMode::NegativeInfinity),
    $negative->round(1, RoundingMode::NegativeInfinity),
);

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;

refnamediv.refpurpose: Gets the square root of an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Return the square root of $this.

listitem.simpara: BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the square root as a new BcMath\Number object.

When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, the BcMath\Number::scale of $this is used. However, in cases such as indivisible division, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result is expanded. Expansion is done only as needed, up to a maximum of +10. This behavior is the same as BcMath\Number::div, so please see that for details.
That is, if the BcMath\Number::scale of $this is 5, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result is between 5 and 15.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
$this is a negative value scale is outside the valid range BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is outside the valid range

example.title: BcMath\Number::sqrt example
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump( new BcMath\Number('2')->sqrt(), new BcMath\Number('2')->sqrt(3), new BcMath\Number('4')->sqrt(), new BcMath\Number('4')->sqrt(3), ); ?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Subtracts an arbitrary precision number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Subtracts num from $this.

listitem.simpara: The value to subtract.
BcMath\Number::scale explicitly specified for calculation results. If null, the BcMath\Number::scale of the calculation result will be set automatically.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the result of subtraction as a new BcMath\Number object.
When the BcMath\Number::scale of the result object is automatically set, the greater BcMath\Number::scale of the two numbers used for subtraction is used.
That is, if the BcMath\Number::scales of two values are 2 and 5 respectively, the BcMath\Number::scale of the result will be 5.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para:
This method throws a ValueError in the following cases:
num is string and not a well-formed BCMath numeric string scale is outside the valid range

example.title: BcMath\Number::sub example when scale is not specified
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

$ret1 = $number->sub(new BcMath\Number('2.34567'));
$ret2 = $number->sub('-3.456');
$ret3 = $number->sub(7);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

example.title: BcMath\Number::sub example of explicitly specifying scale
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = new BcMath\Number('1.234');

$ret1 = $number->sub(new BcMath\Number('2.34567'), 1);
$ret2 = $number->sub('-3.456', 10);
$ret3 = $number->sub(7, 0);

var_dump($number, $ret1, $ret2, $ret3);
?>

preface.title: Introduction
preface.simpara: These functions allow for arbitrary-length integers to be worked with using the GNU MP library.

note.para: Most GMP functions accept GMP number arguments. These are shown in this documentation as GMP objects. Most of these functions will also accept numeric and string arguments, so long as it is possible to convert the latter to a number. Also, if there is a more performant function that can operate on the arguments (integers only), then it will be used instead (this is done transparently). See also the gmp_init function.
The arithmetic, bitwise, and comparison operators may be used with the GMP objects returned from gmp_init and other GMP functions.

warning.simpara: Large integers must be specified as strings - otherwise, PHP will coerce them to floats, resulting in a loss of precision.

section.title: Requirements
section.para: The GMP library can be downloaded from http://gmplib.org/#DOWNLOAD. This site also has the GMP manual available.
section.simpara: At least GMP version 4.2 is required, with some functions requiring a more recent version of the GMP library.
On Windows, MPIR is required instead of GMP.

section.title: Installation
section.para: In order to have these functions available, PHP must be compiled with GMP support by using the --with-gmp option.

appendix.title: Predefined Constants
appendix.simpara: The constants below are defined by this extension, and will only be available when the extension has either been compiled into PHP or dynamically loaded at runtime.

listitem.simpara: The GMP library version
The MPIR library version.

chapter.title: Examples

example.title: Factorial function using GMP
example.programlisting:
<?php
function fact($x) 
{
    $return = 1;
    for ($i=2; $i <= $x; $i++) {
        $return = gmp_mul($return, $i);
    }
    return $return;
}

echo gmp_strval(fact(1000)) . "\n";
?>

chapter.para: This will calculate factorial of 1000 (pretty big number) very fast.

section.title: See Also
section.para: More mathematical functions can be found in the section

refnamediv.refpurpose: Absolute value

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Get the absolute value of a number.

listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns the absolute value of num, as a GMP number.

example.title: gmp_abs example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$abs1 = gmp_abs("274982683358");
$abs2 = gmp_abs("-274982683358");

echo gmp_strval($abs1) . "\n";
echo gmp_strval($abs2) . "\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Clear bit

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Clears (sets to 0) bit index in num. The index starts at 0.

listitem.para: A GMP object.
The index of the bit to clear. Index 0 represents the least significant bit.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: No value is returned.

example.title: gmp_clrbit example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$a = gmp_init("0xff");
gmp_clrbit($a, 0); // index starts at 0, least significant bit
echo gmp_strval($a) . "\n";
?>

note.para: Unlike most of the other GMP functions, gmp_clrbit must be called with a GMP object that already exists (using gmp_init for example). One will not be automatically created.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Compare numbers

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Compares two numbers.

listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).
A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns a positive value if a > b, zero if a = b and a negative value if a < b.

example.title: gmp_cmp example
example.programlisting:
<?php $cmp1 = gmp_cmp("1234", "1000"); // greater than $cmp2 = gmp_cmp("1000", "1234"); // less than $cmp3 = gmp_cmp("1234", "1234"); // equal to

refnamediv.refpurpose: Alias of gmp_div_q

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: This function is an alias of: gmp_div_q.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Divide numbers

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Divides num1 by num2 and returns the integer result.

listitem.para: The number being divided.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

listitem.para: The number that num1 is being divided by.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

listitem.para:
The result rounding is defined by the rounding_mode, which can have the following values:
GMP_ROUND_ZERO: The result is truncated towards 0.
GMP_ROUND_PLUSINF: The result is rounded towards +infinity.
GMP_ROUND_MINUSINF: The result is rounded towards -infinity.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: A GMP object.

example.title: gmp_div_q example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$div1 = gmp_div_q("100", "5");
echo gmp_strval($div1) . "\n";

$div2 = gmp_div_q("1", "3");
echo gmp_strval($div2) . "\n";

$div3 = gmp_div_q("1", "3", GMP_ROUND_PLUSINF);
echo gmp_strval($div3) . "\n";

$div4 = gmp_div_q("-1", "4", GMP_ROUND_PLUSINF);
echo gmp_strval($div4) . "\n";

$div5 = gmp_div_q("-1", "4", GMP_ROUND_MINUSINF);
echo gmp_strval($div5) . "\n";
?>

note.para: This function can also be called as gmp_div.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Divide numbers and get quotient and remainder

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: The function divides num1 by num2.

listitem.para: The number being divided.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

listitem.para: The number that num1 is being divided by.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

listitem.para: See the gmp_div_q function for description of the rounding_mode argument.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns an array, with the first element being [n/d] (the integer result of the division) and the second being (n - [n/d] * d) (the remainder of the division).

example.title: Division of GMP numbers
example.programlisting:
<?php
$a = gmp_init("0x41682179fbf5");
$res = gmp_div_qr($a, "0xDEFE75");
printf("Result is: q - %s, r - %s",
       gmp_strval($res[0]), gmp_strval($res[1]));
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Export to a binary string

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Exports a GMP number to a binary string. This function can handle arbitrarily large numbers beyond the range of PHP's native integer type, with configurable word size and byte order, similar in spirit to pack.
The sign of the number is ignored; exporting a negative number produces the same result as exporting its absolute value.

listitem.simpara: The GMP number to export.
The number of bytes per word in the output. The total length of the returned string will be a multiple of this value. Default value: 1.

A bitmask controlling word order and byte order. Word order: GMP_MSW_FIRST (most significant word first, default) or GMP_LSW_FIRST (least significant word first). Byte order within each word: GMP_NATIVE_ENDIAN (default), GMP_BIG_ENDIAN, or GMP_LITTLE_ENDIAN. Default value: GMP_MSW_FIRST | GMP_NATIVE_ENDIAN.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns a string containing the binary representation of the GMP number. The string is empty if the number is zero.

row.entry: This function no longer returns false on failure.

example.title: gmp_export example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = gmp_init(16705);
echo gmp_export($number) . "\n";
?>

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Calculates factorial (num!) of num.

listitem.para: The factorial number.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: A GMP object.

example.title: gmp_fact example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$fact1 = gmp_fact(5); // 5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1
echo gmp_strval($fact1) . "\n";

$fact2 = gmp_fact(50); // 50 * 49 * 48, ... etc
echo gmp_strval($fact2) . "\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Calculate GCD

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Calculate greatest common divisor of num1 and num2. The result is always positive even if either of, or both, input operands are negative.

listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refnamediv.refpurpose: Calculate GCD and multipliers

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Calculates g, s, and t, such that a*s + b*t = g = gcd(a,b), where gcd is the greatest common divisor. Returns an array with respective elements g, s and t.

This function can be used to solve linear Diophantine equations in two variables. These are equations that allow only integer solutions and have the form: a*x + b*y = c. For more information, go to the "Diophantine Equation" page at MathWorld

listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).
A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: An array of GMP numbers.

example.title: Solving a linear Diophantine equation
example.programlisting:
<?php
// Solve the equation a*s + b*t = g
// where a = 12, b = 21, g = gcd(12, 21) = 3
$a = gmp_init(12);
$b = gmp_init(21);
$g = gmp_gcd($a, $b);
$r = gmp_gcdext($a, $b);

$check_gcd = (gmp_strval($g) == gmp_strval($r['g']));
$eq_res = gmp_add(gmp_mul($a, $r['s']), gmp_mul($b, $r['t']));
$check_res = (gmp_strval($g) == gmp_strval($eq_res));

if ($check_gcd && $check_res) {
    $fmt = "Solution: %d*%d + %d*%d = %d\n";
    printf($fmt, gmp_strval($a), gmp_strval($r['s']), gmp_strval($b),
    gmp_strval($r['t']), gmp_strval($r['g']));
} else {
    echo "Error while solving the equation\n";
}

// output: Solution: 12*2 + 21*-1 = 3
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Create GMP number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Creates a GMP number from an integer or string.

listitem.simpara: An integer or a string. The string representation can be decimal, hexadecimal, octal, or binary.
The base to use for converting a string representation.

An explicit base can be between 2 and 62. For bases up to 36, case is ignored; upper-case and lower-case letters have the same value. For bases 37 to 62, upper-case letter represent the values 10 to 35 and lower-case letter represent the values 36 to 61.

If base is 0 then the actual base is determined from the leading characters of num. If the first two characters are 0x or 0X, the string is interpreted as a hexadecimal integer. If the first two characters are 0b or 0B, the string is interpreted as a binary integer. If the first two characters are 0o or 0O, the string is interpreted as an octal integer. Moreover, if the first character is 0 the string is also interpreted as an octal integer. In all other cases, the string is interpreted as a decimal integer.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: A GMP object.

row.entry: Support for explicit octal prefixes 0o and 0O has been added for num strings. Interpretation of such prefixes when base is 0 has also been added.

example.title: Creating GMP number
example.programlisting:
<?php
$a = gmp_init(123456);
$b = gmp_init("0xFFFFDEBACDFEDF7200");
?>

note.para: It is not necessary to call this function in order to use integers or strings in place of GMP numbers in GMP functions (such as with gmp_add). Function arguments are automatically converted to GMP numbers, if such conversion is possible and needed, using the same rules as gmp_init.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Check if number is "probably prime"

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: The function uses Miller-Rabin's probabilistic test to check if a number is a prime.

listitem.para: The number being checked as a prime.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

listitem.para: Reasonable values of repetitions vary from 5 to 10 (default being 10); a higher value lowers the probability for a non-prime to pass as a "probable" prime.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: If this function returns 0, num is definitely not prime. If it returns 1, then num is "probably" prime. If it returns 2, then num is surely prime.

example.title: gmp_prob_prime example
example.programlisting:
<?php
// definitely not a prime
echo gmp_prob_prime("6") . "\n";

// probably a prime
echo gmp_prob_prime("1111111111111111111") . "\n";

// definitely a prime
echo gmp_prob_prime("11") . "\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Random number

warning.simpara: This function has been DEPRECATED as of PHP 7.2.0, and REMOVED as of PHP 8.0.0. Relying on this function is highly discouraged.

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Generate a random number. The number will be between 0 and (2 ** n) - 1, where n is the number of bits per limb multiplied by limiter. If limiter is negative, negative numbers are generated.

A limb is an internal GMP mechanism. The number of bits in a limb is not static, and can vary from system to system. Generally, the number of bits in a limb is either 32 or 64, but this is not guaranteed.

caution.simpara: This function does not generate cryptographically secure values, and must not be used for cryptographic purposes, or purposes that require returned values to be unguessable.

If cryptographically secure randomness is required, the Random\Randomizer may be used with the Random\Engine\Secure engine. For simple use cases, the random_int and random_bytes functions provide a convenient and secure API that is backed by the operating system’s CSPRNG.

listitem.para: The limiter.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: A random GMP number.

example.title: gmp_random example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$rand1 = gmp_random(1); // random number from 0 to 1 * bits per limb
$rand2 = gmp_random(2); // random number from 0 to 2 * bits per limb

echo gmp_strval($rand1) . "\n";
echo gmp_strval($rand2) . "\n";
?>

refsect1.para: Scans num1, starting with bit start, towards more significant bits, until the first clear bit is found.

listitem.para: The number to scan.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

listitem.para: The starting bit.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns the index of the found bit, as an int. The index starts from 0.

example.title: gmp_scan0 example
example.programlisting:
<?php
// "0" bit is found at position 3. index starts at 0
$s1 = gmp_init("10111", 2);
echo gmp_scan0($s1, 0) . "\n";

// "0" bit is found at position 7. index starts at 5
$s2 = gmp_init("101110000", 2);
echo gmp_scan0($s2, 5) . "\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Scan for 1

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Scans num1, starting with bit start, towards more significant bits, until the first set bit is found.

listitem.para: The number to scan.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

listitem.para: The starting bit.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns the index of the found bit, as an int. If no set bit is found, -1 is returned.

example.title: gmp_scan1 example
example.programlisting:
<?php
// "1" bit is found at position 3. index starts at 0
$s1 = gmp_init("01000", 2);
echo gmp_scan1($s1, 0) . "\n";

// "1" bit is found at position 9. index starts at 5
$s2 = gmp_init("01000001111", 2);
echo gmp_scan1($s2, 5) . "\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Set bit

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Sets bit index in num.

listitem.para: A GMP object.
The index of the bit to set. Index 0 represents the least significant bit.
True to set the bit (set it to 1/on); false to clear the bit (set it to 0/off).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: No value is returned.

example.title: gmp_setbit example - 0 index
example.programlisting:
<?php
$a = gmp_init("2"); //
echo gmp_strval($a), ' -> 0b', gmp_strval($a, 2), "\n";
gmp_setbit($a, 0); // 0b10 now becomes 0b11
echo gmp_strval($a), ' -> 0b', gmp_strval($a, 2), "\n";
?>

example.title: gmp_setbit example - 1 index
example.programlisting:
<?php
$a = gmp_init("0xfd");
echo gmp_strval($a), ' -> 0b', gmp_strval($a, 2), "\n";
gmp_setbit($a, 1); // index starts at 0
echo gmp_strval($a), ' -> 0b', gmp_strval($a, 2), "\n";
?>

example.title: gmp_setbit example - clearing a bit
example.programlisting:
<?php
$a = gmp_init("0xff");
echo gmp_strval($a), ' -> 0b', gmp_strval($a, 2), "\n";
gmp_setbit($a, 0, false); // clear bit at index 0
echo gmp_strval($a), ' -> 0b', gmp_strval($a, 2), "\n";
?>

note.para: Unlike most of the other GMP functions, gmp_setbit must be called with a GMP object that already exists (using gmp_init for example). One will not be automatically created.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Sign of number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Checks the sign of a number.

listitem.para: Either a GMP object, or a numeric string provided that it is possible to convert the latter to an int.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns 1 if num is positive, -1 if num is negative, and 0 if num is zero.

example.title: gmp_sign example
example.programlisting:
<?php
// positive
echo gmp_sign("500") . "\n";

// negative
echo gmp_sign("-500") . "\n";

// zero
echo gmp_sign("0") . "\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Calculate square root

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Calculates square root of num.

listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The integer portion of the square root, as a GMP number.

example.title: gmp_sqrt example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$sqrt1 = gmp_sqrt("9");
$sqrt2 = gmp_sqrt("7");
$sqrt3 = gmp_sqrt("1524157875019052100");

echo gmp_strval($sqrt1) . "\n";
echo gmp_strval($sqrt2) . "\n";
echo gmp_strval($sqrt3) . "\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Square root with remainder

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Calculate the square root of a number, with remainder.

listitem.para: The number being square rooted.
listitem.simpara: A GMP object, an int, or a string that can be interpreted as a number following the same logic as if the string was used in gmp_init with automatic base detection (i.e. when base is equal to 0).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Returns array where first element is the integer square root of num and the second is the remainder (i.e., the difference between num and the first element squared).

example.title: gmp_sqrtrem example
example.programlisting:
<?php
list($sqrt1, $sqrt1rem) = gmp_sqrtrem("9");
list($sqrt2, $sqrt2rem) = gmp_sqrtrem("7");
list($sqrt3, $sqrt3rem) = gmp_sqrtrem("1048576");

echo gmp_strval($sqrt1) . ", " . gmp_strval($sqrt1rem) . "\n";
echo gmp_strval($sqrt2) . ", " . gmp_strval($sqrt2rem) . "\n";
echo gmp_strval($sqrt3) . ", " . gmp_strval($sqrt3rem) . "\n";
?>

section.title: Introduction
section.para: A GMP number. These objects support overloaded arithmetic, bitwise and comparison operators.

note.para: No object-oriented interface is provided to manipulate GMP objects. Please use the procedural GMP API.

row.entry: A GMP object can now be cast to bool; an object representing 0 is cast to false, and any other value to true. Previously, casting to bool emitted an E_RECOVERABLE_ERROR.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Create GMP number

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Creates a GMP number from an integer or string.

listitem.simpara: An integer or a string. The string representation can be decimal, hexadecimal, octal, or binary.
The base to use for converting a string representation.

An explicit base can be between 2 and 62. For bases up to 36, case is ignored; upper-case and lower-case letters have the same value. For bases 37 to 62, upper-case letter represent the values 10 to 35 and lower-case letter represent the values 36 to 61.

If base is 0 then the actual base is determined from the leading characters of num. If the first two characters are 0x or 0X, the string is interpreted as a hexadecimal integer. If the first two characters are 0b or 0B, the string is interpreted as a binary integer. If the first two characters are 0o or 0O, the string is interpreted as an octal integer. Moreover, if the first character is 0 the string is also interpreted as an octal integer. In all other cases, the string is interpreted as a decimal integer.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Convert a number between arbitrary bases

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns a string containing num represented in base to_base. The base in which num is given is specified in from_base. Both from_base and to_base have to be between 2 and 36, inclusive. Digits in numbers with a base higher than 10 will be represented with the letters a-z, with a meaning 10, b meaning 11 and z meaning 35. The case of the letters doesn't matter, i.e. num is interpreted case-insensitively.

warning.simpara: base_convert may lose precision on large numbers due to properties related to the internal float type used. Please see the Floating point numbers section in the manual for more specific information and limitations.

listitem.para: The number to convert. Any invalid characters in num are silently ignored. As of PHP 7.4.0 supplying any invalid characters is deprecated.
The base num is in
The base to convert num to

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: num converted to base to_base

row.entry: Passing invalid characters will now generate a deprecation notice. The result will still be computed as if the invalid characters did not exist.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Binary to decimal

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the decimal equivalent of the binary number represented by the binary_string argument.
bindec converts a binary number to an int or, if needed for size reasons, float.
bindec interprets all binary_string values as unsigned integers. This is because bindec sees the most significant bit as another order of magnitude rather than as the sign bit.

listitem.para: The binary string to convert. Any invalid characters in binary_string are silently ignored. As of PHP 7.4.0 supplying any invalid characters is deprecated.

warning.para: The parameter must be a string. Using other data types will produce unexpected results.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The decimal value of binary_string

row.entry: Passing invalid characters will now generate a deprecation notice. The result will still be computed as if the invalid characters did not exist.

example.title: bindec example
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo bindec('110011') . "\n";
echo bindec('000110011') . "\n";

echo bindec('111');
?>

example.title: bindec interprets input as unsigned integers
example.programlisting:
<?php
/*
 * The lesson from this example is in the output
 * rather than the PHP code itself.
 */

$magnitude_lower = pow(2, (PHP_INT_SIZE * 8) - 2);
p($magnitude_lower - 1);
p($magnitude_lower, 'See the rollover?  Watch it next time around...');

p(PHP_INT_MAX, 'PHP_INT_MAX');
p(~PHP_INT_MAX, 'interpreted to be one more than PHP_INT_MAX');

if (PHP_INT_SIZE == 4) {
    $note = 'interpreted to be the largest unsigned integer';
} else {
    $note = 'interpreted to be the largest unsigned integer
              (18446744073709551615) but skewed by float precision';
}
p(-1, $note);


function p($input, $note = '') {
    echo "input:        $input\n";

    $format = '%0' . (PHP_INT_SIZE * 8) . 'b';
    $bin = sprintf($format, $input);
    echo "binary:       $bin\n";

    ini_set('precision', 20);  // For readability on 64 bit boxes.
    $dec = bindec($bin);
    echo 'bindec():     ' . $dec . "\n";

    if ($note) {
        echo "NOTE:         $note\n";
    }

    echo "\n";
}
?>
example.simpara: Output of the above example on 32 bit machines:
example.screen:
input: 1073741823 binary: 00111111111111111111111111111111 bindec(): 1073741823
input: 1073741824 binary: 01000000000000000000000000000000 bindec(): 1073741824 NOTE: See the rollover? Watch it next time around...
input: 2147483647 binary: 01111111111111111111111111111111 bindec(): 2147483647 NOTE: PHP_INT_MAX
input: -2147483648 binary: 10000000000000000000000000000000 bindec(): 2147483648 NOTE: interpreted to be one more than PHP_INT_MAX
input: -1 binary: 11111111111111111111111111111111 bindec(): 4294967295 NOTE: interpreted to be the largest unsigned integer
example.simpara: Output of the above example on 64 bit machines:

note.para: The function can convert numbers that are too large to fit into the platforms int type, larger values are returned as float in that case.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Decimal to hexadecimal

refsect1.para: Returns a string containing a hexadecimal representation of the given unsigned num argument.

listitem.para: The decimal value to convert.
As PHP's int type is signed, but dechex deals with unsigned integers, negative integers will be treated as though they were unsigned.

<?php
// The output below assumes a 32-bit platform.
// Note that the output is the same for all values.
echo dechex(-1)."\n";
echo dechex(PHP_INT_MAX * 2 + 1)."\n";
echo dechex(pow(2, 32) - 1)."\n";
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns the floating point remainder (modulo) of the division of the arguments

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the floating point remainder of dividing the dividend (num1) by the divisor (num2). The remainder (r) is defined as: num1 = i * num2 + r, for some integer i. If num2 is non-zero, r has the same sign as num1 and a magnitude less than the magnitude of num2.

listitem.para: The dividend
The divisor

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The floating point remainder of num1/num2. NAN (float) if the second argument is 0.

example.title: Using fmod
example.programlisting:
<?php
$x = 5.7;
$y = 1.3;
$r = fmod($x, $y);
// $r equals 0.5, because 4 * 1.3 + 0.5 = 5.7

var_dump($x, $y, $r);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Raise one number to the power of another, according to IEEE 754

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns the floating point result of raising num to the power of exponent. If num is zero and exponent is less than zero, then INF is returned.

listitem.simpara: The base to use.
The exponent.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns a float corresponding to $num$exponent.

example.title: fpow example
example.programlisting:
<?php
var_dump(fpow(10, 2));
var_dump(fpow(0, -3));
var_dump(fpow(-1, 5.5));
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Hexadecimal to decimal

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the decimal equivalent of the hexadecimal number represented by the hex_string argument. hexdec converts a hexadecimal string to a decimal number.
hexdec will ignore any non-hexadecimal characters it encounters. As of PHP 7.4.0 supplying any invalid characters is deprecated.

listitem.para: The hexadecimal string to convert

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The decimal representation of hex_string

row.entry: Passing invalid characters will now generate a deprecation notice. The result will still be computed as if the invalid characters did not exist.

example.title: hexdec example
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump(hexdec("ee")); // prints "int(238)" var_dump(hexdec("a0")); // prints "int(160)" ?>

example.title: hexdec with Invalid Characters
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump(hexdec("See")); // print "int(238)" var_dump(hexdec("that")); // print "int(10)" ?>

note.para: The function can convert numbers that are too large to fit into the platforms int type, larger values are returned as float in that case.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Calculate the length of the hypotenuse of a right-angle triangle

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: hypot returns the length of the hypotenuse of a right-angle triangle with sides of length x and y, or the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin. This is equivalent to sqrt($x*$x + $y*$y).

listitem.para: Length of first side
Length of second side

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: Calculated length of the hypotenuse

refnamediv.refpurpose: Integer division

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the integer quotient of the division of num1 by num2.

listitem.para: Number to be divided.
Number which divides the num1.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The integer quotient of the division of num1 by num2.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: If num2 is 0, a DivisionByZeroError exception is thrown. If the num1 is PHP_INT_MIN and the num2 is -1, then an ArithmeticError exception is thrown.

example.title: intdiv example
example.programlisting:
<?php
var_dump(intdiv(3, 2));
var_dump(intdiv(-3, 2));
var_dump(intdiv(3, -2));
var_dump(intdiv(-3, -2));
var_dump(intdiv(PHP_INT_MAX, PHP_INT_MAX));
var_dump(intdiv(PHP_INT_MIN, PHP_INT_MIN));
?>
example.screen: int(1) int(-1) int(-1) int(1) int(1) int(1)

example.title: intdiv Example With Invalid Divisor
example.programlisting:
<?php
try {
    intdiv(PHP_INT_MIN, -1);
} catch (Error $e) {
    echo get_class($e), ': ', $e->getMessage(), PHP_EOL;
}

try {
    intdiv(1, 0);
} catch (Error $e) {
    echo get_class($e), ': ', $e->getMessage(), PHP_EOL;
}
?>
example.screen: ArithmeticError: Division of PHP_INT_MIN by -1 is not an integer DivisionByZeroError: Division by zero

refnamediv.refpurpose: Checks whether a float is finite

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns whether the given num is a finite float.
A finite float is neither NAN (is_nan), nor infinite (is_infinite).

listitem.para: The float to check

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: true if num is none of NAN, INF, -INF, else false.

example.title: is_finite example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$float = 1.2345;
var_dump($float, is_finite($float));

$nan = sqrt(-1);
var_dump($nan, is_finite($nan));

$inf = 1e308 * 2;
var_dump($inf, is_finite($inf));
?>
example.screen: float(1.2345) bool(true) float(NAN) bool(false) float(INF) bool(false)

refnamediv.refpurpose: Checks whether a float is infinite

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns whether the given num is either INF or -INF.

listitem.para: The float to check

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: true if num is either INF or -INF, else false.

example.title: is_infinite example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$inf = 1e308 * 2;

var_dump($inf, is_infinite($inf));

$negative_inf = -$inf;

var_dump($negative_inf, is_infinite($negative_inf));
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Checks whether a float is NAN

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns whether the given num is NAN (Not A Number).

NAN is returned from mathematical operations that are undefined, for example when passing parameters outside of function’s input domain. The square root (sqrt) is only defined for positive numbers, passing a negative number will result in NAN. Other examples of operations returning NAN are dividing INF by INF and any operation involving an existing NAN value.

note.para: Despite its name of Not A Number, NAN is a valid value of type float.

caution.para: NAN does not compare equal to NAN. To check whether a float is NAN, is_nan must be used. Checking $float === NAN will not work.

listitem.para: The float to check

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: true if num is NAN, else false.

example.title: is_nan example
example.programlisting:
<?php
$nan = sqrt(-1);

var_dump($nan, is_nan($nan));
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Natural logarithm

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: If the optional base parameter is specified, log returns logbase num, otherwise log returns the natural logarithm of num.

listitem.para: The value to calculate the logarithm for
The optional logarithmic base to use (defaults to 'e' and so to the natural logarithm).

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The logarithm of num to base, if given, or the natural logarithm.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Base-10 logarithm

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the base-10 logarithm of num.

listitem.para: The argument to process

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The base-10 logarithm of num

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns log(1 + number), computed in a way that is accurate even when the value of number is close to zero

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: log1p returns log(1 + num) computed in a way that is accurate even when the value of num is close to zero. log might only return log(1) in this case due to lack of precision.

listitem.para: The argument to process

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: log(1 + num)

refnamediv.refpurpose: Find highest value

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Alternative signature (not supported with named arguments):
refsect1.para: If the first and only parameter is an array, max returns the highest value in that array. If at least two parameters are provided, max returns the biggest of these values.

note.para: Values of different types will be compared using the standard comparison rules. For instance, a non-numeric string will be compared to an int as though it were 0, but multiple non-numeric string values will be compared alphanumerically. The actual value returned will be of the original type with no conversion applied.

caution.simpara: Be careful when passing arguments of different types because max can produce unpredictable results.

listitem.para: Any comparable value.
Any comparable values.
An array containing the values.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: max returns the parameter value considered "highest" according to standard comparisons. If multiple values of different types evaluate as equal (e.g. 0 and 'abc') the first provided to the function will be returned.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: If an empty array is passed, max throws a ValueError.

row.entry: max throws a ValueError on failure now; previously, false was returned and an E_WARNING error was emitted.
As string to number comparisons were changed, max no longer returns a different value based on the argument order in those cases.

example.title: Example uses of max
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo max(2, 3, 1, 6, 7), PHP_EOL;  // 7
echo max(array(2, 4, 5)), PHP_EOL; // 5

// Here we are comparing -1 < 0, so 'hello' is the highest value
echo max('hello', -1), PHP_EOL;    // hello

// With multiple arrays of different lengths, max returns the longest
$val = max(array(2, 2, 2), array(1, 1, 1, 1)); // array(1, 1, 1, 1)
var_dump($val);

// Multiple arrays of the same length are compared from left to right
// so in our example: 2 == 2, but 5 > 4
$val = max(array(2, 4, 8), array(2, 5, 1)); // array(2, 5, 1)
var_dump($val);

// If both an array and non-array are given, the array will be returned
// as comparisons treat arrays as greater than any other value
$val = max('string', array(2, 5, 7), 42);   // array(2, 5, 7)
var_dump($val);

// If one argument is NULL or a boolean, it will be compared against
// other values using the rule FALSE < TRUE regardless of the other types involved
// In the below example, -10 is treated as TRUE in the comparison
$val = max(-10, FALSE); // -10
var_dump($val);

// 0, on the other hand, is treated as FALSE, so is "lower than" TRUE
$val = max(0, TRUE); // TRUE
var_dump($val);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Find lowest value

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Alternative signature (not supported with named arguments):
refsect1.para: If the first and only parameter is an array, min returns the lowest value in that array. If at least two parameters are provided, min returns the smallest of these values.

note.para: Values of different types will be compared using the standard comparison rules. For instance, a non-numeric string will be compared to an int as though it were 0, but multiple non-numeric string values will be compared alphanumerically. The actual value returned will be of the original type with no conversion applied.

caution.simpara: Be careful when passing arguments of different types because min can produce unpredictable results.

listitem.para: Any comparable value.
Any comparable values.
An array containing the values.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: min returns the parameter value considered "lowest" according to standard comparisons. If multiple values of different types evaluate as equal (e.g. 0 and 'abc') the first provided to the function will be returned.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.para: If an empty array is passed, min throws a ValueError.

row.entry: min throws a ValueError on failure now; previously, false was returned and an E_WARNING error was emitted.
As string to number comparisons were changed, min no longer returns a different value based on the argument order in those cases.

example.title: Example uses of min
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo min(2, 3, 1, 6, 7), PHP_EOL;  // 1
echo min(array(2, 4, 5)), PHP_EOL; // 2

// Here we are comparing -1 < 0, so -1 is the lowest value
echo min('hello', -1), PHP_EOL;    // -1

// With multiple arrays of different lengths, min returns the shortest
$val = min(array(2, 2, 2), array(1, 1, 1, 1)); // array(2, 2, 2)
var_dump($val);

// Multiple arrays of the same length are compared from left to right
// so in our example: 2 == 2, but 4 < 5
$val = min(array(2, 4, 8), array(2, 5, 1)); // array(2, 4, 8)
var_dump($val);

// If both an array and non-array are given, the array is never returned
// as comparisons treat arrays as greater than any other value
$val = min('string', array(2, 5, 7), 42);   // string
var_dump($val);

// If one argument is NULL or a boolean, it will be compared against
// other values using the rules FALSE < TRUE and NULL == FALSE regardless of the 
// other types involved
// In the below examples, both -10 and 10 are treated as TRUE in the comparison
$val = min(-10, FALSE, 10); // FALSE
var_dump($val);

$val = min(-10, NULL, 10);  // NULL
var_dump($val);

// 0, on the other hand, is treated as FALSE, so is "lower than" TRUE
$val = min(0, TRUE); // 0
var_dump($val);
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Octal to decimal

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the decimal equivalent of the octal number represented by the octal_string argument.

listitem.para: The octal string to convert. Any invalid characters in octal_string are silently ignored. As of PHP 7.4.0 supplying any invalid characters is deprecated.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The decimal representation of octal_string

row.entry: Passing invalid characters will now generate a deprecation notice. The result will still be computed as if the invalid characters did not exist.

example.title: octdec example
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo octdec('77') . "\n";
echo octdec(decoct(45));
?>

note.para: The function can convert numbers that are too large to fit into the platforms int type, larger values are returned as float in that case.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Get value of pi

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns an approximation of pi. Also, you can use the M_PI constant which yields identical results to pi.

refsect1.title: Parameters
refsect1.simpara: This function has no parameters.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The value of pi as float.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Exponential expression

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns num raised to the power of exponent.

note.para: It is possible to use the ** operator instead.

listitem.para: The base to use
The exponent

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: num raised to the power of exponent. If both arguments are non-negative integers and the result can be represented as an integer, the result will be returned with int type, otherwise it will be returned as a float.
PHP-Extensions may override the behaviour of this operation and make it return an object.

row.entry: Raising 0 to a negative exponent is now deprecated.

example.title: Some examples of pow
example.programlisting:
<?php
var_dump(pow(2, 8)); // int(256) echo pow(-1, 20), PHP_EOL; // 1 echo pow(0, 0), PHP_EOL; // 1 echo pow(10, -1), PHP_EOL; // 0.1
echo pow(-1, 5.5), PHP_EOL; // NAN ?>

example.title: Examples of pow With GMP Extension Object
example.programlisting: <?php var_dump(pow(new GMP("3"), new GMP("2"))); // object(GMP) ?>

note.para: This function will convert all input to a number, even non-scalar values, which could lead to weird results.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Converts the radian number to the equivalent number in degrees

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: This function converts num from radian to degrees.

listitem.para: A radian value

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The equivalent of num in degrees

example.title: rad2deg example
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo rad2deg(M_PI_4); // 45
?>

refnamediv.refpurpose: Rounds a float

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Returns the rounded value of num to specified precision (number of digits after the decimal point). precision can also be negative or zero (default).

listitem.para: The value to round.
The optional number of decimal digits to round to.
If the precision is positive, num is rounded to precision significant digits after the decimal point.

If the precision is negative, num is rounded to precision significant digits before the decimal point, i.e. to the nearest multiple of pow(10, -$precision), e.g. for a precision of -1 num is rounded to tens, for a precision of -2 to hundreds, etc.

Use RoundingMode or one of the following constants to specify the mode in which rounding occurs.
Constants Description
PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP
Rounds num away from zero when it is half way there, making 1.5 into 2 and -1.5 into -2.
PHP_ROUND_HALF_DOWN
Rounds num towards zero when it is half way there, making 1.5 into 1 and -1.5 into -1.
PHP_ROUND_HALF_EVEN
Rounds num towards the nearest even value when it is half way there, making both 1.5 and 2.5 into 2.
PHP_ROUND_HALF_ODD
Rounds num towards the nearest odd value when it is half way there, making 1.5 into 1 and 2.5 into 3.
However, please note that some newly added modes only exist in RoundingMode.

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.para: The value rounded to the given precision as a float.

refsect1.title: Errors/Exceptions
refsect1.simpara: The function throws a ValueError if mode is invalid. Prior to PHP 8.4.0, an invalid mode would silently default to PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP.

row.entry: Four new rounding modes have been added.
Now throws a ValueError if mode is invalid.
num no longer accepts internal objects which support numeric conversion.

example.title: round examples
example.programlisting:
<?php
var_dump(round(3.4));
var_dump(round(3.5));
var_dump(round(3.6));
var_dump(round(3.6, 0));
var_dump(round(5.045, 2));
var_dump(round(5.055, 2));
var_dump(round(345, -2));
var_dump(round(345, -3));
var_dump(round(678, -2));
var_dump(round(678, -3));
?>
example.screen: float(3) float(4) float(4) float(4) float(5.05) float(5.06) float(300) float(0) float(700) float(1000)

example.title: How precision affects a float
example.programlisting:
<?php
$number = 135.79;

var_dump(round($number, 3));
var_dump(round($number, 2));
var_dump(round($number, 1));
var_dump(round($number, 0));
var_dump(round($number, -1));
var_dump(round($number, -2));
var_dump(round($number, -3));
?>
example.screen: float(135.79) float(135.79) float(135.8) float(136) float(140) float(100) float(0)

example.title: mode examples
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo 'Rounding modes with 9.5' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(round(9.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP));
var_dump(round(9.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_DOWN));
var_dump(round(9.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_EVEN));
var_dump(round(9.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_ODD));

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Rounding modes with 8.5' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(round(8.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP));
var_dump(round(8.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_DOWN));
var_dump(round(8.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_EVEN));
var_dump(round(8.5, 0, PHP_ROUND_HALF_ODD));
?>
example.screen:
Rounding modes with 9.5 float(10) float(9) float(10) float(9)
Rounding modes with 8.5 float(9) float(8) float(8) float(9)

example.title: mode with precision examples
example.programlisting:
<?php
echo 'Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(round( 1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP));
var_dump(round(-1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP));

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_DOWN with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(round( 1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_DOWN));
var_dump(round(-1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_DOWN));

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_EVEN with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(round( 1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_EVEN));
var_dump(round(-1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_EVEN));

echo PHP_EOL;
echo 'Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_ODD with 1 decimal digit precision' . PHP_EOL;
var_dump(round( 1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_ODD));
var_dump(round(-1.55, 1, PHP_ROUND_HALF_ODD));
?>
example.screen:
Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_UP with 1 decimal digit precision float(1.6) float(-1.6)
Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_DOWN with 1 decimal digit precision float(1.5) float(-1.5)
Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_EVEN with 1 decimal digit precision float(1.6) float(-1.6)
Using PHP_ROUND_HALF_ODD with 1 decimal digit precision float(1.5) float(-1.5)

example.title: Example of using RoundingMode
example.programlisting:
<?php
foreach (RoundingMode::cases() as $mode) {
    foreach ([
        8.5,
        9.5,
        -3.5,
    ] as $number) {
        printf("%-17s: %+.17g -> %+.17g\n", $mode->name, $number, round($number, 0, $mode));
    }
    echo "\n";
}
?>
example.screen:
HalfAwayFromZero : +8.5 -> +9 HalfAwayFromZero : +9.5 -> +10 HalfAwayFromZero : -3.5 -> -4
HalfTowardsZero : +8.5 -> +8 HalfTowardsZero : +9.5 -> +9 HalfTowardsZero : -3.5 -> -3
HalfEven : +8.5 -> +8 HalfEven : +9.5 -> +10 HalfEven : -3.5 -> -4
HalfOdd : +8.5 -> +9 HalfOdd : +9.5 -> +9 HalfOdd : -3.5 -> -3
TowardsZero : +8.5 -> +8 TowardsZero : +9.5 -> +9 TowardsZero : -3.5 -> -3
AwayFromZero : +8.5 -> +9 AwayFromZero : +9.5 -> +10 AwayFromZero : -3.5 -> -4
NegativeInfinity : +8.5 -> +8 NegativeInfinity : +9.5 -> +9 NegativeInfinity : -3.5 -> -4
PositiveInfinity : +8.5 -> +9 PositiveInfinity : +9.5 -> +10 PositiveInfinity : -3.5 -> -3

preface.title: Introduction
preface.para:
This extension is unmaintained.
This is the statistics extension. It contains few dozens of functions useful for statistical computations. It is a wrapper around 2 scientific libraries, namely DCDFLIB (Library of C routines for Cumulative Distributions Functions, Inverses, and Other parameters) by B. Brown & J. Lavato and RANDLIB by Barry Brown, James Lavato & Kathy Russell. Includes CD and PD functions.

section.title: Requirements
section.para: No external libraries are needed. The extension comes bundled with the libraries used.

section.title: Installation
section.para: This PECL extension is not bundled with PHP.
This extension is considered unmaintained and dead. However, the source code for this extension is still available within PECL SVN here: https://pecl.php.net/package/stats.
Windows binaries (DLL files) for this PECL extension are available from the PECL website.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Returns the absolute deviation of an array of values

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns the absolute deviation of the values in a.

listitem.simpara: The input array

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns the absolute deviation of the values in a, or false if a is empty or is not an array.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Calculates any one parameter of the beta distribution given values for the others

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns the cumulative distribution function, its inverse, or one of its parameters, of the beta distribution. The kind of the return value and parameters (par1, par2, and par3) are determined by which.
refsect1.para:
The following table lists the return value and parameters by which. CDF, x, alpha, and beta denotes cumulative distribution function, the value of the random variable, and shape parameters of the beta distribution, respectively.
Return value and parameters
which Return value par1 par2 par3
1 CDF x alpha beta
2 x CDF alpha beta
3 alpha x CDF beta
4 beta x CDF alpha

listitem.simpara: The first parameter
The second parameter
The third parameter
The flag to determine what to be calculated

refsect1.title: Return Values
refsect1.simpara: Returns CDF, x, alpha, or beta, determined by which.

refnamediv.refpurpose: Calculates any one parameter of the binomial distribution given values for the others

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.simpara: Returns the cumulative distribution function, its inverse, or one of its parameters, of the binomial distribution. The kind of the return value and parameters (par1, par2, and par3) are determined by which.
refsect1.para:
The following table lists the return value and parameters by which. CDF, x, n, and p denotes cumulative distribution function, the number of successes, the number of trials, and the success rate for each trial, respectively.
Return value and parameters
which Return value par1 par2 par3
1 CDF x n p
2 x CDF n p
3 n x CDF p
4 p x CDF n

listitem.simpara: The first parameter
